0.title: Esther: The Hidden Hand
0.overview:
The message. Esther shows that God rules the world and keeps his people even when he cannot be seen. A whole nation is sentenced to death, and no prophet speaks. Instead an orphan girl becomes queen, a king cannot sleep, a forgotten good deed is read aloud, and a gallows built for one man is used for another. On the very day set for the Jews’ destruction, “the reverse occurred” (9:1). God is never named in the book, yet by the end no reader can doubt whose hand has been on every page. So God is present in most of his people’s lives: not in burning bushes, but in the timing of things.

When and where. In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and let the exiles go home, but many Jews stayed, scattered through an empire that ran “from India to Ethiopia” (1:1). Esther is their story. Its king, Ahasuerus, is the one the Greeks called Xerxes, who reigned from 486 to 465 BC. The events run from about 483 BC (1:3) to about 474 BC (3:7), between the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 1–6) and Ezra’s journey to Jerusalem (Ezra 7); a generation later Nehemiah served Xerxes’ son in the same palace at Susa, a Persian capital in what is now south-west Iran (Nehemiah 1:1). The book’s picture of the court, the royal couriers and laws that “may not be repealed” (1:19) fits what we know of Persia.

Background: the writer. The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited the Great Assembly, the council said to have followed Ezra; some have guessed Mordecai. The writer looks back on Xerxes’ whole reign (10:2), knows Persian ways at first hand, and points readers to the royal chronicles. Many scholars date it much later, in the Greek period, and read it as a historical novel. This commentary holds that a Jew of the Persian empire wrote it, probably within a few generations of the events, from trustworthy records.

The kind of writing. Esther is narrative history, told with great skill and full of irony and reversal: a man who wanted the king’s honour forced to give it to his enemy, a lot cast to choose a day of death that gives a festival its name. Read it slowly and notice the “coincidences”; that is where the author wants you to see God. That silence is deliberate. The Greek translators later added passages with prayers and the name of the Lord, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles keep; our Bibles follow the Hebrew, and this commentary does not count those additions as Scripture.

How the book makes its case. The book turns on one sleepless night. Before it, danger grows. Esther, an orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is taken into the king’s harem and made queen in place of Vashti, keeping her people secret; Mordecai saves the king’s life and is forgotten [1–2]. Haman the Agagite is promoted, Mordecai will not bow, and Haman wins a decree to kill every Jew in the empire on a day chosen by lot [3]. Mordecai urges Esther to plead: “who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (4:14). She answers, “if I perish, I perish” (4:16), goes in uncalled and is spared, while Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai [4–5]. Then “On that night the king could not sleep” (6:1), and everything begins to turn. Haman must parade Mordecai through the city in royal robes [6], and at Esther’s second feast he is unmasked and hanged on his own gallows [7]. The first decree cannot be revoked, so a second is written giving the Jews the right to defend themselves [8]. On the appointed day they prevail, and the feast of Purim is set up to remember it for ever [9]. Mordecai ends second to the king, seeking “the welfare of his people” (10:3) [10].

The old war. The family names carry an old story. Mordecai is “son of Kish, a Benjaminite” (2:5), of the clan of King Saul; Haman is an Agagite, almost certainly of the line of Agag, the Amalekite king whom Saul spared against God’s command (1 Samuel 15:9). Of Amalek God had said, “The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation” (Exodus 17:16). Five centuries later the two families meet again, and this time the Jews “laid no hand on the plunder” (9:10), where Saul had kept it.

Is Esther history, and is it Scripture? Some doubt the story because Greek historians name Xerxes’ queen as Amestris. But a Persian king had several wives, the four-year gap between chapters 1 and 2 (1:3; 2:16) fits the years Xerxes spent at war in Greece, and the surviving Persian records are too sparse to settle it. Others doubted that a book without God’s name belongs in the Bible; some in the early church hesitated, and Luther wished it did not exist. But Jews and Christians alike received it, and its silence is part of its message. With the historic confessions, this commentary holds that Scripture as first given is without error, and reads Esther as a true account of what God did.

Heroes or warnings? Esther hides her people and becomes a pagan king’s wife, where Daniel had refused even the king’s food; the narrator makes no comment. Chapter 9 records the Jews killing their enemies, but in defence against those who came to kill them. This commentary’s view is that these are records, not patterns. God does not wait for his people to do everything well before he saves them, and the church is given no such sword, for “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Where it leads: to Christ. The New Testament never quotes Esther, and the book makes no promise of a Messiah, so the link must not be forced. But it is real. First, by promise kept: God had sworn to Abraham, “him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). Had Haman succeeded there would have been no people for the Christ to be born into; God kept them because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Second, by pattern: Esther went in uncalled for a condemned people, ready to perish; Christ went knowing he would die, and because of him we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). Haman’s tree, raised for the righteous man, held the guilty; at the cross it was reversed: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Third, by the need it exposes: a sentence that could not be revoked could only be answered by another word from the king. In Christ that word is spoken: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). And the hidden hand of Esther is the hand that delivered Jesus up “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and turned the worst day into the best.

For us. Most Christians never see a miracle. Esther shows that God is no less at work in sleepless nights and forgotten kindnesses, and that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). It calls us to courage where God has put us, for such a time as this. And it gives hope to a church that often looks weak: its enemies may write their decrees, but they do not have the last word. Purim was kept with feasting, “gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor” (9:22). Those whom Christ has rescued from a far greater sentence have even more reason for joy.

1.title: The Banquet, the Queen, and the Empty Throne
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces,<sup>2</sup>in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel,<sup>3</sup>in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him,<sup>4</sup>while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.<sup>5</sup>And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace.<sup>6</sup>There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones.<sup>7</sup>Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king.<sup>8</sup>And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.<sup>9</sup>Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.<sup>10</sup>On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus,<sup>11</sup>to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at.<sup>12</sup>But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.<sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment,<sup>14</sup>the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom):<sup>15</sup>"According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"<sup>16</sup>Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.<sup>17</sup>For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'<sup>18</sup>This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty.<sup>19</sup>If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she.<sup>20</sup>So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."<sup>21</sup>This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed.<sup>22</sup>He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
1.overview:
Where we are. Esther opens not in Jerusalem but at the centre of the Persian empire, in the palace at Susa, in about 483 BC. Many Jews have stayed in the lands of their exile instead of going home (see the introduction), and this first chapter does not even mention them.

The message. The greatest king on earth puts his glory on show and cannot rule his own household, and his wounded pride leaves the throne beside him empty. God is not named, yet he is already at work: the drunken anger, the panicked advice and the law that cannot be repealed are clearing a place for the queen he will use to save his people. Human power is loud and hollow; God’s rule is quiet and sure.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small people scattered through a vast pagan empire, at the mercy of kings and their courts, with no prophet speaking (see the introduction). This chapter teaches them to look at the powers of their world without awe, and to watch for the hand the story does not name.

How the chapter makes its case. First the display: half a year of glory for the empire’s great men, then a week of lavish feasting for all Susa, while Vashti feasts the women (vv. 1–9). Then the crack in it: merry with wine, the king sends for his queen to show off her beauty, and she refuses (vv. 10–12). Finally the farce: the council of seven turns one refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire, Vashti is deposed by a law that cannot be repealed, her place is to go “to another who is better than she”, and the imperial post carries the news to every province (vv. 13–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by contrast, and by the need the chapter exposes. Ahasuerus summons his queen to display her for his own glory; Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her”, to make her beautiful (Ephesians 5:25). And the God who stays hidden in this chapter did not stay hidden for ever: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18).

For us. The powers that seem to run the world are not as solid as they look, and they are not in charge. When God seems absent from the news and from your own life, he is not idle. And you are not loved by a king who uses you, but by one who spent himself for you.
1.theology:
God is not named in this chapter, and he is never absent from it. He rules through a drunken king's vanity, a queen's refusal and a counsellor's panic as surely as through a parted sea. Two things here drive the rest of the story: the law that cannot be repealed, and the counsellor’s words, which echo Samuel’s words to Saul about Agag.

Ahasuerus summons his queen to display her beauty for his glory; Christ gives himself for his bride to make her beautiful (Eph 5:25-27, see on vv. 10-12).
1.examples: The chapter is full of power that turns out hollow. Half a year of display came three years before Xerxes' fleet was lost at Salamis; the king who ruled 127 provinces could not bring his wife across a courtyard; and the empire's whole postal system was set moving to announce that husbands must be respected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Riches of His Royal Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens on the most powerful man in the world at the height of his glory, and invites us to look past it. Ahasuerus sits on his throne in Susa, ruling 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia (vv. 1–2). For 180 days he shows his officials and army “the riches of his royal glory” (vv. 3–4). Then he gives all Susa, great and small, a seven-day feast in the palace garden, among couches of gold and silver and wine in golden cups, where no one is compelled to drink (vv. 5–8). Queen Vashti gives a feast for the women in a palace that belongs to the king (v. 9). Everything here belongs to him, or so he thinks.
verseByVerse.theology: The book opens on the most powerful man in the world at the height of his glory, and teaches the reader to look for the hand the story does not name.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces, in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel, in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him, while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story opens at the summit of the most powerful throne on earth, where the reader must learn to watch for a hand the book never names.

In the days of Ahasuerus. Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the name the Greeks wrote as Xerxes, who reigned from 486 to 465 BC over an empire from the Indus to the upper Nile (see the introduction). In this palace at Susa, a generation later, a Jew named Nehemiah would hand Xerxes’ son his wine (Nehemiah 1:1; 2:1).

For many days, 180 days. The display lasted half a year. The third year of Xerxes was 483 BC, and many think the 180 days were partly a gathering of the empire’s leaders to plan his invasion of Greece. Within three years that campaign had met disaster when his fleet was beaten at Salamis (480 BC). The glory on display was not as solid as it looked.

A book where no one prays. Here God is never named and no one is said to pray. We must learn to see his hand in the timing of a feast, a refusal and a sleepless night, which is how most believers live most of their days.
verseByVerse.note: Susa was the Persian kings' winter capital, in modern Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace. There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones. Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king. And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king feasts the whole city in dazzling luxury, and even the drinking runs by decree.

Couches of gold and silver. The narrator lingers on the furnishings as if walking us through a showroom: silver rods, marble pillars, couches of gold and silver on a pavement of porphyry and mother-of-pearl. Everyone in the city, great and small, is drinking from gold.

Drinking was according to this edict. This is a book full of decrees, in which what the king desires is done. And there is irony: at this feast no one is compelled to drink; in a few verses one person will be commanded to come, and will not.

A feast. The Hebrew word for feast comes about twenty times in this short book. Kings decide things at feasts in Esther, usually after much wine, and the whole story will turn on two small feasts given by a queen.

Uncertain wording. Several words for the fabrics and stones in verse 6 are rare in the Bible, and some are probably borrowed from Persian. The picture is clear, rich hangings and a mosaic floor of costly stones, but “porphyry” and “mother-of-pearl” are translators’ best guesses. Nothing in the meaning depends on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary: Queen Vashti holds a feast of her own, but in a palace that belongs to the king. Everything in this world belongs to him: the palace, the cups, the provinces and, he assumes, the queen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king who rules the world cannot command his own wife, and his pride leaves the throne beside him empty. On the seventh day, “when the heart of the king was merry with wine”, he sends seven eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti, wearing her crown, to show her beauty to the peoples and the princes (vv. 10–11). She refuses, and his anger burns within him (v. 12). The narrator does not say why she refused and neither praises nor blames her. He shows us a husband who treats his wife as one more treasure to display, and the empty place his anger is about to make.
verseByVerse.theology: The book does not tell us why she refused; it tells us that an empty throne was the result.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus, to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at. But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drunk and proud, the king sends for his queen to be put on show like his golden cups, and her refusal leaves him shamed and furious.

To bring Queen Vashti before the king. A week of wine, a hall full of men, and the king sends for his wife to be looked at: one more possession, the finest one. “Lovely to look at” is exactly what will be said of Esther in the next chapter (2:7). In this court, that is what a woman is for.

But Queen Vashti refused to come. The narrator does not tell us why. He neither praises Vashti nor blames her, and we should not fill the silence with our own story. But he has shown us the summons, and we can see it for what it is.

Another King. This king called for his queen to show off her beauty for his own glory. There is another King who gave himself for his bride, “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27), and whose feast is “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). When the wine ran out at a village wedding, he quietly made more and “manifested his glory” (John 2:11). One king uses his bride to display his glory. The other spends his glory to make his bride beautiful.

For a wife in a hard marriage. A reader may be living in a marriage where what is asked of her is degrading. Scripture’s call to wives, “submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord”, sits directly beside the call to husbands: “love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:22, 25). A summons to be paraded before drunken men is the opposite of that love, and no one is bound to obey a command to shame or sin: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Where it has become abuse, tell a pastor or another trusted believer, and if you are in danger, seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — So That It May Not Be Repealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A law that cannot be repealed deposes a queen, and the comedy hides the danger that will drive the book. Publicly refused, the king turns to his seven wise men and asks what the law requires (vv. 13–15). Memucan warns that every wife in the empire will now despise her husband, and proposes an unrepealable decree: Vashti will never again come before the king, and her royal position will go “to another who is better than she”, words that echo Samuel’s sentence on Saul (vv. 16–20). The king agrees, and letters go to every province in every script, “that every man be master in his own household” (vv. 21–22). The same kind of law and the same couriers will soon carry a sentence of death.
verseByVerse.theology: The decree is a comedy here, where it deposes a queen; the same kind of law will be a terror in chapter 3.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment, the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom): "According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Publicly refused, the ruler of the world turns to his lawyers, and the narrator means us to smile.

The seven princes of Persia and Media. Seven named princes, “who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom”: the kind of council of seven that sent Ezra to Jerusalem under the next king (Ezra 7:14). The most powerful man on earth cannot manage his own household without a meeting of the cabinet, and he wants it done “according to the law”.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.' This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty. If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she. So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Memucan turns one refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire, and proposes a law that cannot be repealed.

Not only against the king. Memucan’s real fear is for the officials themselves: “This very day”, he says, their own wives will be repeating the story.

So that it may not be repealed. Here, for the first time, is the rule the whole plot will hang on. The law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed even by the king who made it (Daniel 6:8, 15). In chapter 3 such a law will sentence a nation to death, and even the king will not be able to take it back (8:8).

Another who is better than she. When Saul spared Agag king of the Amalekites, Samuel told him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you” (1 Samuel 15:28). A Persian lawyer who had almost certainly never heard of Samuel uses the same words. And the story of Saul and Agag is about to be played again: Mordecai will be introduced as a Benjaminite, “son of Kish” (2:5), and his enemy as “Haman the Agagite” (3:1). The narrator never says God is arranging things. He lets the echo of Samuel’s words say it.

verseByVerse.quote: This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed. He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A law can depose a queen, but it cannot make anyone honour anyone.

He sent letters to all the royal provinces. The whole imperial post, in every script from India to Ethiopia, is set moving to announce that husbands are in charge: the most powerful state on earth making itself ridiculous. Respect cannot be decreed, and love still less.

Remember those couriers. The same postal system will carry a decree of death to every province in chapter 3, and a decree of life in chapter 8. And the throne beside the king is now empty. Nobody in Susa that night was thinking about the Jews. Someone was.

Where is God when he does not show himself? Many say they would believe if God would only make himself plain: a voice, a sign, one unmistakable intervention. Esther is written for people who never get one. Its world looks very like ours, power, money, parties, politics, and no visible God anywhere; read only the surface, and the story is chance and clever people. Blaise Pascal argued that a religion which did not say God is hidden could not be true, because a God who overwhelmed us with proof would compel the head without winning the heart; he gives light enough to be found by those who seek him, and leaves room to be missed by those who would rather not. Esther teaches us to read life by watching the timing. But it also leaves us waiting for the hidden God to stop hiding, and the New Testament says he did: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). In Jesus the God of Esther stepped out from behind the curtain, and his face was the face of one who came to save a condemned people.

Uncertain wording. The last clause, that every man should “speak according to the language of his people”, is obscure. It probably means that in a household of mixed nationality the husband’s language was to be spoken at home, one more mark of who ruled it. Others take it loosely: the husband was to have the last word at home. Either way, the decree’s point is clear.

keyVerse.quote: And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter full of pride and wine, this is where the story turns: the throne beside the king is made empty for someone not yet named. The words echo Samuel’s sentence on Saul for sparing Agag (1 Samuel 15:28), and they announce the theme of the whole book, that God is quietly preparing the place and the person long before the danger appears.

1.reflection:
The chapter lingers over 180 days of royal display and a week of golden cups (vv. 1–8), yet within a few years Xerxes’ great invasion of Greece had failed. What kinds of power and glory impress us most today, and how does this chapter teach us to see them?

The king treats his queen as one more treasure to show off (vv. 10–11). Where do you see people being used for someone else’s glory, at work, online or at home? How does Christ’s love for his bride, giving himself to make her beautiful (Ephesians 5:25–27), challenge the way we treat one another?

God is never named in this chapter, yet the empty throne will prove to be part of his plan. Looking back, where can you see God at work in events that seemed ordinary, or even foolish, at the time?

Many people say they would believe if God would only show himself plainly. How would you answer them from this chapter, and from the claim of John 1:18 that in Jesus God has made himself known?

2.title: The Girl From Exile: Esther Comes to the Throne
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her.<sup>2</sup>Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king.<sup>3</sup>And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them.<sup>4</sup>And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.<sup>5</sup>Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,<sup>6</sup>who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away.<sup>7</sup>He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.<sup>8</sup>So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women.<sup>9</sup>And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
2.overview:
Where we are. Some years after Vashti’s fall (the great feast was in Xerxes’ third year; Esther is crowned in his seventh), the king’s anger has cooled and the empty throne must be filled. Here we meet the two Jews on whom the whole story will turn.

The message. God puts his servants where they will be needed long before anyone knows the need. Through an empire’s crude search for a new queen, an orphan of the exile is raised to the throne of Persia, and a good deed is written into the king’s records and forgotten. God does not approve all that happens to them, but he works through it, and nothing done for him is lost.

Why it was said. The first readers were scattered among the nations, often powerless, living in situations they had not chosen (see the introduction). This chapter shows them God’s favour reaching his people even there, unseen and unannounced.

How the chapter makes its case. The plan: gather beautiful young women from every province, and whoever pleases the king will be queen (vv. 1–4). The people: Mordecai, a Benjaminite with names from Saul’s family, and his orphaned cousin Hadassah, Esther, whom he has raised as his daughter (vv. 5–7). The favour: taken into the harem, Esther wins Hegai’s kindness and, on Mordecai’s orders, keeps her people secret (vv. 8–11). After the year of preparation and the one night that decided each girl’s life (vv. 12–14), the king loves Esther “more than all the women” and crowns her (vv. 15–18). Last, Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king; the men are hanged, and the deed is recorded in the chronicles, unrewarded (vv. 19–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God. The orphan taken in as a daughter is a small picture of the adoption God gives in his Son (Galatians 4:4–5). The King of the gospel is the opposite of Ahasuerus: he does not choose one bride for her beauty and leave the rest waiting, for “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). And the deed filed and forgotten shows a God who remembers: he “is not unjust so as to overlook your work” (Hebrews 6:10).

For us. You may be somewhere you did not choose to be, and not handling it perfectly. God does not wait for his people to get everything right before he uses them. And the kindness nobody thanked you for has not been forgotten by him.
2.theology: God is still unnamed, and his hand is everywhere: an orphan placed in the palace, favour given as the LORD once gave it to Joseph (Gen 39:21), a good deed filed in an archive to be found at the right moment. He works through people in situations they did not choose and do not always handle well, without approving everything they do. And nothing done for him is lost, even when no one says thank you.
2.examples: Small details carry the chapter: a cousin who walked past the harem wall every day to ask how she was, a girl who took only what she was advised to take, and a man who saved the king's life and got nothing but a line in the annals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Let the Young Woman Who Pleases the King Be Queen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The empire sets about replacing its queen by gathering young women from 127 provinces like tribute, and into that cruel machinery God is about to set an orphan. The king’s anger cools, and he remembers Vashti and the decree that cannot be undone (v. 1). His young men propose a search: officers in every province are to bring beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa, into the custody of Hegai, “and let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti” (vv. 2–4). The plan pleases the king. The narrator neither condemns it nor dresses it up.
verseByVerse.theology: The empire begins to replace a queen by gathering young women from 127 provinces like tribute.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her. Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king. And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them. And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trapped by his own decree, the king agrees to fill the empty throne by gathering girls from the whole empire.

He remembered Vashti. The wine and the anger have worn off, and he remembers her and “what had been decreed against her”. The law meant to show his power cannot be repealed.

Let beautiful young virgins be sought out. Call it what it is: girls taken from their families across the empire for the king to choose from. The narrator does not stop to condemn it, nor does he dress it up. And into the middle of it he is about to set a Jewish orphan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An orphan of the exile is raised to the throne of Persia, and the favour that carries her there is given by someone the book never names. Mordecai, a Benjaminite with names from Saul’s family, has raised his cousin Hadassah, Esther, as his own daughter (vv. 5–7). Taken into the harem, she wins Hegai’s favour and, on Mordecai’s orders, keeps her people secret, while he walks past the harem every day for news (vv. 8–11). After a year of beautifying, each young woman goes in to the king for one night (vv. 12–14). Esther asks for nothing but what Hegai advises, and “the king loved Esther more than all the women” and made her queen (vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The favor and grace Esther wins in this chapter are given by someone. The book never says who.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away. He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai, a Jew of Saul’s family line, has raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter.

Son of Shimei, son of Kish. Every Israelite reader would recognise the names. “There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish”: that is how the story of Saul begins (1 Samuel 9:1). Shimei was the man of Saul’s house who cursed David as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 16:5). Mordecai comes from the family of Israel’s first king. Keep that in mind until the next chapter introduces his enemy.

Carried away with Jeconiah. Jeconiah was taken into exile by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12), and Esther is taken to the king in 479 BC (v. 16), 118 years later. So Mordecai was born in Persia, a descendant of the exiles who never went home (see the box below).

Hadassah, that is Esther. She has two names. Hadassah is Hebrew for myrtle, the tree Isaiah promised would grow where thorns had been: “instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle” (Isaiah 55:13). Esther is her Persian name.

For anyone raised by another. Many readers have lost a parent, or were raised by someone who did not have to take them in. Mordecai’s kindness is a small picture of a larger one: God sent his Son “to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5), and the Son promised, “I will not leave you as orphans” (John 14:18).

Uncertain wording. “Who had been carried away” could refer to Mordecai or to Kish, the name just before it; since the exile was over a century earlier, it most naturally means Kish, his great-grandfather. The name Esther probably comes from the Persian word for star, though some link it with the goddess Ishtar.
verseByVerse.note: Kish and Shimei are both names from Saul’s family.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women. And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food, and with seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and advanced her and her young women to the best place in the harem. Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther wins favour she did not seek, and keeps her people secret.

Esther also was taken. The verb is passive. She did not enter a contest; she was collected.

And won his favor. The word here is hesed, the Old Testament’s great word for God’s steadfast love. A eunuch in a pagan harem shows it to a Jewish girl, and the text does not say why.

Esther had not made known her people. Why Mordecai insisted on silence we are not told; the next chapter will show what one man in power could do to a people he hated. He could not get her out, so every day he walked past the wall that held her, asking for news: a picture of helpless love that will not stop caring.

A hard question. Esther eats the king’s food, where Daniel, taken to a pagan court a century earlier, “resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food” (Daniel 1:8). She hides her people, and in time she will spend a night with a pagan king. The narrator makes no comment. God does not wait for his people to handle everything well before he uses them. That is not permission to compromise. It is mercy for those who already have (see the note on vv. 15–18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women— when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she desired to take with her from the harem to the king's palace. In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A year of preparation led to one night, and for most of the young women to a lifetime of waiting.

The regular period of their beautifying. Twelve months of oils and spices, then one evening with the king. For every girl not chosen, what followed was her life: a concubine for ever, never to marry, never to go home, waiting to be “summoned by name” and almost certainly never summoned. The narrator states it in one flat sentence and lets the cruelty speak for itself.

For anyone who was used. Some readers know this from the inside: they were taken, used, or treated as a thing to be enjoyed and set aside. Scripture does not blame Esther or the other girls for what was done to them, and neither should we; the shame belongs to those who took them. Abuse is never acceptable. Anyone in danger now should seek safety at once and tell someone who can help, and a pastor or biblical counsellor can walk with you in the long work of healing. And the gospel’s King is the opposite of this one. He does not choose one bride for her beauty and leave the rest waiting for ever: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: When the turn came for Esther the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her. And when Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign, the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Then the king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants; it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asking for nothing more than she is advised, Esther wins the king’s love and the crown, through a favour the narrator never explains.

Esther the daughter of Abihail. As she goes in, the narrator gives the orphan’s father a name: she is somebody’s daughter. Every other girl could take “whatever she desired” (v. 13); Esther took only what she was advised. She did not grasp for more.

In the seventh year of his reign. Four years have passed since the feast of chapter 1, the years in which Xerxes led his armies into Greece and came home defeated. The king who sat down with Esther had lost a war.

Grace and favor. These are the words Genesis uses of Joseph in prison: “the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor” (Genesis 39:21). In Genesis the giver is named. In Esther he is not. That is how this whole book talks about God.

It was Esther’s feast. An orphan of the exile, with no family but a cousin at the gate, wears the crown of Persia, and nobody in the palace knows she is a Jew.

Where Christians differ: how should we judge Esther? Many have held her up as a model of faith throughout; others see a young woman far from God’s law, hiding her identity and marrying a pagan, whom God used in spite of herself. This commentary’s view: the narrator gives no verdict, and we should supply neither a heroic one nor a harsh one. She was taken, not a volunteer (v. 8). Marriage to a pagan went against the spirit of the law (Deuteronomy 7:3–4), but Scripture records it honestly, as it records Joseph’s Egyptian marriage, without approving every circumstance. These chapters are a record, not a pattern (see the introduction), and their hero is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — Recorded in the Book of the Chronicles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai saves the king’s life, and his deed goes into a book and is forgotten by everyone but the One the book never names. Mordecai sits at the king’s gate, and Esther, now queen, still keeps her people secret, obeying him as she did as a child (vv. 19–20). Two eunuchs who guard the king’s door plot to kill him; Mordecai learns of it and tells Esther, who tells the king in his name. The men are hanged, and the matter is “recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king” (vv. 21–23). There is no reward, no promotion, not even thanks: not yet.
verseByVerse.theology: The deed goes into a book and is forgotten by everyone but the One the book never names.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as queen, Esther stays hidden and obeys the cousin who raised her.

The virgins were gathered together the second time. A second gathering, after Esther was crowned: the harem went on filling. Her crown did not make her secure, and in chapter 4 she will say she has not been called to the king for thirty days (4:11).

Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate. The gate was where officials sat and business was done, so Mordecai probably held some post in the king’s service. Queen of Persia, Esther still did as her cousin told her, “just as when she was brought up by him”, and that habit of trust between them is what the whole deliverance will depend on.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And this came to the knowledge of Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai. When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai saves the king’s life and receives nothing; the deed is filed and forgotten, but not by God.

Bigthan and Teresh. Two guards of the king’s door plotted to murder him, and Mordecai’s warning reached the king “in the name of Mordecai”. The word for gallows is simply wood, a tree; it will appear again, fifty cubits high, in chapter 5.

Recorded in the book of the chronicles. The chapter ends on a book. No reward, no promotion, not even thanks: a clerk wrote a line in the annals, and everybody forgot.

A deed unthanked. Many know how it feels when a costly good deed vanishes without thanks. But with God no such deed is forgotten: “a book of remembrance was written before him” (Malachi 3:16). The Persian clerk thought he was filing a routine report. He was placing the most important page of the story exactly where a sleepless king would one day find it (6:1–2).

keyVerse.quote: the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.
keyVerse.note: The orphan of the exile is crowned, and the narrator describes it in the words Genesis uses of God’s kindness to Joseph, without naming the giver. Years before anyone has heard of Haman’s plan, God has quietly put his servant on the throne, which is how this whole book shows his care for his people.

2.reflection:
Esther was taken into a situation she did not choose, and the narrator does not pretend it was good (vv. 8, 12–14). How does it help to know that God can work through circumstances he does not approve? How can we keep that truth from becoming an excuse for compromise?

Mordecai took in an orphan as his daughter and walked past the harem wall every day for news of her (vv. 7, 11). Who has cared for you like that, and whom might God be calling you to care for? How does his adoption of us in Christ (Galatians 4:4–7) shape that care?

Esther kept her people secret and ate the king’s food, where Daniel refused (Daniel 1:8). Where are you tempted to keep your faith quiet in order to fit in? When is discretion wise, and when does it become hiding?

Mordecai’s good deed went unthanked and was simply filed away (v. 23). How do you respond when faithfulness goes unnoticed, and what difference does it make that God does not forget (Malachi 3:16; Hebrews 6:10)?

3.title: The Decree of Death: Haman's Plot Against the Jews
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.<sup>2</sup>And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage.<sup>3</sup>Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?"<sup>4</sup>And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.<sup>5</sup>And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury.<sup>6</sup>But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.<sup>7</sup>In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.<sup>8</sup>Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them.<sup>9</sup>If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."<sup>10</sup>So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews.<sup>11</sup>And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."<sup>12</sup>Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.<sup>13</sup>Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.<sup>14</sup>A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day.<sup>15</sup>The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
3.overview:
Where we are. Five years have passed since Esther was crowned, and Mordecai’s rescue of the king lies forgotten in the chronicles (2:23). Now the enemy enters the story.

The message. The ancient hatred of God’s people comes back to life in a Persian official, and with the king’s ring it becomes law: every Jew in the empire is to die on one day. Yet the chapter is full of quiet signs that the enemy is not in control. The lot he consults falls eleven months away, and his decree is written on the eve of Passover, the feast of God’s greatest deliverance. Evil can write laws; it cannot govern the lot.

Why it was said. The first readers knew what it was to be a scattered minority, “different”, at the mercy of rulers who could be turned against them (see the introduction). This chapter names that danger honestly, and shows them who still holds the dice.

How the chapter makes its case. Haman the Agagite is raised above all, and everyone bows except Mordecai, who has told them he is a Jew (vv. 1–4). Haman, “filled with fury”, resolves to destroy not one man but his whole people (vv. 5–6). Lots are cast, and they fall on Adar, eleven months away (v. 7). Haman slanders “a certain people” and offers the king a fortune; the king hands over his signet ring and the people without asking who they are (vv. 8–11). The decree goes out in every language, to kill all Jews, young and old, on one day (vv. 12–14), and while the king and Haman sit down to drink, Susa is thrown into confusion (v. 15).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. Behind Haman stands the oldest enmity, between the serpent and the offspring of the woman (Genesis 3:15). God had promised that in Abraham’s family “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3); to destroy the Jews would have been to destroy the family from which the Christ would come. And the closing scene, powerful men content over the condemned, returns at the cross, where “Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day” (Luke 23:12), and where God turned the worst verdict ever passed into the gospel.

For us. Hatred of God’s people is not new, and faithfulness can make things worse before they get better. But the decrees of the powerful are not the last word. Christians slandered as “a certain people” should neither panic nor hate in return, but trust the One who governs every lot.
3.theology:
The ancient war with Amalek, left unfinished by Saul (1 Sam 15), returns: an Agagite turns the sentence once given against Amalek on the people of God. Behind it is the oldest enmity of all, the attempt to destroy the people from whom the Messiah would come.

Haman cast lots for the day of death, but the lots were not his to govern. The decree written on the eve of Passover would be undone, and its lots would name the feast of deliverance.
3.examples: The chapter turns on injustice and indifference. The man who saved the king got nothing, while Haman was promoted for nothing. Haman never named the people he wanted destroyed, and the king gave them away without asking who they were, his own queen among them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Mordecai Did Not Bow Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The son of Kish will not bow to the Agagite, and an old war comes back to life in the Persian court. For no reason we are told, the king promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials and commands everyone to bow to him (vv. 1–2). Mordecai alone refuses. Day after day his colleagues press him, and when they report him to Haman, they mention that he has told them he is a Jew (vv. 3–4). Haman is “filled with fury”, but killing one man is beneath him; he sets out “to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” (vv. 5–6). A personal grudge becomes a plan to wipe out a people.
verseByVerse.theology: The son of Kish will not bow to the Agagite, and an old war comes back to life in the Persian court.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king raises Haman above everyone, and with one word, “Agagite”, the old war between Israel and Amalek returns.

After these things. After Mordecai saved the king’s life and received nothing (2:23). The man who deserved honour is left at the gate; a man of whom we know nothing is raised above all. The world often looks like that. The book will not leave it there.

Haman the Agagite. For a Jewish reader, the one word is enough. Agag was king of the Amalekites, who fell on Israel’s stragglers in the wilderness, “when you were faint and weary” (Deuteronomy 25:18), and of whom God said, “The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation” (Exodus 17:16). Saul, son of Kish, was sent to finish that war and spared Agag (1 Samuel 15:9). More than five hundred years later Mordecai, son of Kish, meets Haman, almost certainly of the line of Agag (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: An Agagite: probably a descendant of Agag, king of the Amalekites, whom Saul spared.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage. Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?" And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every official bows to Haman except Mordecai, whose only explanation is that he is a Jew.

But Mordecai did not bow down. Israelites bowed to kings and great men without sin: David bowed to Saul with his face to the ground (1 Samuel 24:8), and Abraham bowed to the Hittites (Genesis 23:7). The only reason the text gives is in verse 4: “he had told them that he was a Jew”. A Jew, son of Kish, would not bow to an Agagite.

Day after day. The pressure of colleagues: everybody else does it; why won’t you? Most of us know it at work. Mordecai stood in it quietly, and it cost far more than he could have guessed.

When faithfulness costs. Faithfulness does not always make things safer, and sometimes it puts others at risk too: Mordecai’s refusal would bring a death sentence on every Jew in the empire. Jesus told his disciples to expect such things: “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18). He went that way first, and he does not send his people into it alone.

Where Christians differ: why did Mordecai refuse, and was he right? Some think bowing to Haman meant giving a man divine honour, like the golden image in Daniel 3; the later Greek additions to Esther give Mordecai a prayer saying so. Others see only pride or the old enmity, and think his stubbornness endangered his people. This commentary’s view: the narrator gives his Jewishness as the only reason, sets the scene inside the war with Amalek, and never says Mordecai was wrong. The book presents his refusal as loyalty to his people and their God, not mere pride, and so should we.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury. But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Haman’s fury one man’s refusal becomes a plan to destroy a whole people.

He disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. Killing one man was beneath Haman’s dignity; a grievance that size needed a nation to satisfy it. That has been the logic of many genocides since: a personal hatred given the power of a state.

The oldest war. Behind this hatred the Bible sees the enmity between the serpent and the offspring of the woman (Genesis 3:15). To destroy all the Jews would have been to destroy the family from which the Messiah was to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — To Destroy, to Kill, and to Annihilate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enemy of the Jews turns his hatred into law, but the dates betray a higher hand. In Nisan, the month of Passover, lots are cast before Haman to choose the day, and the lot falls on Adar, eleven months away (v. 7). Haman tells the king of “a certain people” whose laws are different and who do not keep the king’s, and offers ten thousand talents of silver for their destruction; the king hands him the signet ring and the people (vv. 8–11). On the eve of Passover the decree is written in every language, to kill all Jews, young and old, on one day (vv. 12–14). The king and Haman sit down to drink, while the city of Susa is thrown into confusion (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The Jews of the empire would hear their death sentence as they prepared to remember their deliverance from Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman casts lots for the day of destruction, and the lot, which is in the LORD’s hands, falls nearly a year away.

In the first month. The twelfth year is five years after Esther was crowned (2:16). And the month is Nisan, the month of Passover, when every Jewish household remembered the night God struck Egypt and brought his people out. In that month an Agagite sat casting lots to find the day to wipe them out.

They cast Pur. Pur is a foreign word, explained in the verse itself, and it will give the festival its name: Purim, Lots (9:24–26). Haman consulted chance to choose the day of death, and the lot fell eleven months away, time for everything that follows. Proverbs had already said who governs the dice: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

Uncertain wording. “Day after day … month after month” is compressed. It probably means that lots were cast for each day and month in turn until one fell on the twelfth month, though some think the casting itself went on for months. Pur is borrowed from Akkadian, meaning a lot; the day chosen appears in verse 13.
verseByVerse.note: Pur is the word for “lot” — the origin of the name Purim.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them. If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman wins the king’s consent with a speech that never names its victims, mixes truth with lies, and ends with money.

A certain people. Listen to how it is done. He never names them. He mixes truth with lies: their laws were different, for they kept a Sabbath, ate differently and worshipped one God; but “they do not keep the king’s laws” was false, except for one man at one gate refusing one bow. And he closes with the argument that moves kings: it does not pay to tolerate them.

I will pay 10,000 talents of silver. Haman offers a fortune to satisfy a grudge. By the Greek historian Herodotus’s reckoning, the whole empire paid the king about 14,500 talents of silver a year in tribute, so Haman was offering roughly two-thirds of that. He probably meant to recover it from the plunder of the Jews (v. 13).

The church and the charge. Christians should recognise it. The church too is a people scattered abroad, “elect exiles of the dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1), with laws of its own, often accused of not keeping the king’s.

Tolerance with a price tag. Haman makes an argument modern people find reasonable. He does not say he hates the Jews; he says they are different, will not fit in, and are bad for business. Our culture prizes tolerance and rightly recoils from Haman. But tolerance can turn: a society can welcome difference while it costs nothing, then decide that people whose consciences will not bend are a problem to be managed. Real tolerance is not having no convictions; it is how you treat people whose convictions you think are wrong. Its strength comes not from believing that nothing is true, which in the end protects no one, but from a gospel in which God loved his enemies (Romans 5:10) and told his people to bless those who curse them. Christians, so often the “certain people” of Haman’s speech, have at times been the majority making it. The cross judges both: there the powers of the day agreed that one man who would not fit was better out of the way, and he died praying for them.
verseByVerse.note: Ten thousand talents of silver is about 340 metric tons (a talent was about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without a question, the king hands Haman his ring and a whole people, his own queen among them.

His signet ring. The ring made a document the king’s own: the power of life and death over millions. And the narrator gives Haman his title for the first time: “the enemy of the Jews”.

The money is given to you. The king does not ask who this people is or what they have done. He seems to wave the silver away, though the sum is remembered later (4:7; 7:4), and hands a nation to the man who hates them. It is not even cruelty; it is indifference, which has killed as many as cruelty ever has.
verseByVerse.note: The signet ring sealed royal decrees with the king’s authority.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring. Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eve of Passover the decree goes to every province: every Jew, young and old, is to be killed on one day and plundered.

The thirteenth day of the first month. The Passover lambs were killed on the fourteenth (Exodus 12:6). The decree of death was written on the eve of Passover, and it would reach Jewish homes as they gathered to remember that God had once struck down the firstborn of their oppressors and spared theirs.

To destroy, to kill, and to annihilate. Three verbs, so that no one could misunderstand. And the list, “young and old, women and children”, is the list Saul was given against Amalek: “kill both man and woman, child and infant” (1 Samuel 15:3). Saul did not carry out that sentence on Agag’s people; now an Agagite writes it against the people of Saul. The plunder was the bribe: whoever killed a Jew could keep his house. The postal system that carried the letters about Vashti now carries a death sentence to every Jewish family from India to Ethiopia, and they have eleven months to wait for it.

What about the sentence on Amalek? That old sentence troubles readers. It was God’s judgment, once, on one nation that had made a practice of preying on the weak and weary (Deuteronomy 25:17–19), carried out by Israel as the Judge’s servant, and never a pattern for anyone else. Haman’s decree is the opposite: private hatred dressed up as law.

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day. The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The decree is posted, the powerful drink and the city is shaken, but the months the decree leaves belong to God.

To be ready for that day. In every town it was posted for the neighbours to read: be ready.

The king and Haman sat down to drink. One sentence holds two scenes: inside, two powerful men with their cups, business concluded; outside, a city in confusion, for even pagan Susa was shaken. It is the picture of the powerful condemning the innocent and sitting down content. The Gospels have another such scene: when the innocent Son of God had been sent from one ruler to another, “Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day” (Luke 23:12).

What the decree cannot do. The decree can only name a day eleven months away. It cannot stop the One who governs every lot from working in those months. The Jews of Susa went to bed under a law that could not be repealed, not knowing that a Jew was wearing the queen’s crown, and that God had put her there five years before the danger existed.

keyVerse.quote: In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
keyVerse.note: Haman thinks he is consulting chance, but the lot falls eleven months away, leaving time for everything God will do. The month of casting is Passover month, and the word Pur will give the festival of deliverance its name. The verse quietly answers the whole chapter: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

3.reflection:
Mordecai would not bow, and his colleagues pressed him “day after day” (v. 4). Where do you feel pressure to go along with what everyone else does? How can we tell faithful conviction from mere stubbornness or pride?

Haman’s speech never names the people, mixes truth with lies and ends with money (vv. 8–9). Where do you hear arguments like it today, against Christians or against others? How should believers, who have so often been “a certain people”, treat those who differ from them?

The king handed over a whole people without asking who they were (vv. 10–11). How can indifference do as much harm as cruelty? Where might God be calling you to ask questions instead of looking away?

The decree was written on the eve of Passover, and the lot fell eleven months away (vv. 7, 12). How does believing that the lot’s “every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33) help you face news that seems to have the last word?

4.title: For Such a Time as This: The Hinge of the Book
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry.<sup>2</sup>He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.<sup>3</sup>And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.<sup>4</sup>When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.<sup>5</sup>Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was.<sup>6</sup>Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,<sup>7</sup>and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.<sup>8</sup>Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people.<sup>9</sup>And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.<sup>10</sup>Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say,<sup>11</sup>"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days."<sup>12</sup>And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.<sup>13</sup>Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.<sup>14</sup>For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"<sup>15</sup>Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai,<sup>16</sup>"Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."<sup>17</sup>Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
4.overview:
Where we are. The decree of death has gone out to every province, and the king and Haman have sat down to drink (3:15). Now Mordecai and the Jews learn what has been done, while Esther, safe in the palace, does not yet know.

The message. God’s purpose to save his people cannot fail, and the people he has placed are still called to act. Deliverance will come, Mordecai says, whatever Esther does; and yet she may have come to the kingdom for this very moment. Faith does not wait to be sure of the outcome. It takes up the risk God has put in its path and leaves the result with him: “if I perish, I perish”.

Why it was said. A scattered people under sentence, with no prophet among them, needed to know that their crying out was not wasted and that the place each of them held was no accident (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Mordecai mourns in sackcloth at the king’s gate, and the Jews in every province fast and weep (vv. 1–3). Esther sends him clothes; he sends her the decree and tells her to plead for her people (vv. 4–9). She explains that to go to the king uncalled is death, and she has not been called for thirty days (vv. 10–12). Mordecai answers that the palace will not save her, that relief will rise “from another place”, and asks, “who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (vv. 13–14). Esther calls for a three-day fast and resolves to go, and from now on it is she who gives the orders (vv. 15–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and clearly. Esther goes uncalled to the throne to plead for a condemned people, ready to die. Christ went to the cross “knowing all that would happen to him” (John 18:4), and did die, under the sentence that was ours, and now “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Because of him the sceptre is always held out to those who come in his name: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

For us. God has put you in a family, a job, a place where you can speak for others, and it is not an accident. You will not be the one who saves God’s people, for he will do that; but you may be given the honour of being used, and Christ has already gone in before you.
4.theology:
God's purpose to preserve his people is certain, and the people he places are still called to act; neither truth cancels the other. The chapter never names God and is full of him: sackcloth, fasting and the who knows of the prophets are the language of a people crying to the only one who can reverse a sentence.

Esther risks death to plead for a condemned people. Christ went knowing he would die, bore the sentence, and now holds the sceptre out to all who come through him (see on vv. 15-16).
4.examples: Esther's first instinct was to send Mordecai clothes, as if a change of clothes could remove the trouble. By the end of the chapter the girl who had always obeyed him is giving him his orders, and walking toward a throne that may kill her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Loud and Bitter Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A whole people in sackcloth, fasting and crying out: in a book that never mentions prayer, it is hard to read this as anything else. When Mordecai learns of the decree he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and cries aloud through the city as far as the king’s gate, where mourners may not enter (vv. 1–2). In every province the Jews mourn with fasting and weeping (v. 3). Esther, not yet knowing why, sends him clothes, and he refuses them (v. 4).
