Through her servant Hathach he tells her everything, sends her a copy of the decree, and commands her to go to the king and plead for her people (vv. 5–9).
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people in sackcloth, fasting, crying out: in a book that never mentions prayer, it is hard to read this as anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry. He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai makes his grief public, crying aloud through the city in sackcloth, up to the gate where mourning was not allowed.

Mordecai tore his clothes. This is no private grief. He goes into the middle of the city in sackcloth and ashes, crying aloud, and everyone in Susa can see what the king’s decree means.

A loud and bitter cry. The words may be old ones. Many readers hear in them the cry of Esau when Jacob had taken his blessing: “he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry” (Genesis 27:34). Amalek was Esau’s grandson (Genesis 36:12). Now an Agagite, of Amalek’s line, has drawn the same cry out of a son of Jacob.

No one was allowed to enter. The Persian palace had a rule: no grief inside. The king was not to be troubled by mourning, so Mordecai goes as far as he is allowed and cries at the door.

The throne the Christian approaches. At that throne mourners are not kept at the gate; Christ calls them blessed: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). He came “to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning” (Isaiah 61:3). No one needs to change out of sackcloth to come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In every province the Jews mourn and fast: a whole nation doing what people do when they have no one left to cry to but God.

In every province. Behind the couriers, town after town, the Jews put on sackcloth. Picture a Jewish family in a village a thousand miles from Susa reading the notice on the wall: on a day in Adar, eleven months from now, your neighbours may kill you and keep your house.

Fasting and weeping. Prayer is not mentioned; it does not need to be. Fasting and weeping are the words of Joel’s call to a people under judgment: “return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them. Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was. Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther’s first instinct is to cover the trouble with clean clothes, but Mordecai will not take off the sackcloth until she knows why he wears it.

She sent garments to clothe Mordecai. Esther does not yet know about the decree, only that Mordecai is in sackcloth at the gate. Her instinct is to get him into proper clothes: fix the outside, and perhaps the trouble will go away. He will not have it. The sackcloth is the message. Joel’s call was to “rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13), and no change of clothes can deal with a decree of death.

Hathach went out to Mordecai. From here the whole conversation passes through a go-between. The queen cannot go out; Mordecai cannot come in. Every word between them is carried across the square by a servant.

verseByVerse.quote: and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews. Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people. And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai sends Esther the facts and the decree itself, and commands her to give up her secret and plead for her people.

The exact sum of money. Mordecai knew the exact sum (3:9); a man at the king’s gate hears things. He wants Esther to know exactly what her people are worth to Haman.

Plead with him on behalf of her people. For years Mordecai had told her to keep her people secret (2:10, 20). Now she must give up the secret that protected her. And to plead is the work of intercession, one person speaking up for others: a queen standing between a king and a condemned people, as Christ stands for his own, who “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — For Such a Time as This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two convictions stand side by side: God’s people will be delivered whatever Esther does, and Esther is where she is for a reason. She explains the law of the inner court: anyone who goes to the king uncalled dies, unless he holds out the golden sceptre, and she has not been called for thirty days (vv. 10–12). Mordecai answers that the palace will not save her, that if she keeps silent relief will rise “from another place” while she and her father’s house perish, and that she may have “come to the kingdom for such a time as this” (vv. 13–14). God does not need her, and he has placed her.
verseByVerse.theology: Two convictions in one breath: God's people will be delivered whatever Esther does; and Esther is where she is for a reason. Neither cancels the other. God does not need her, and he has placed her.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say, "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days." And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther answers honestly: to go to the king uncalled is death, and she has not been called for a month.

There is but one law. Esther is not making excuses; she is telling Mordecai the truth about the palace. To walk into the inner court uncalled is to walk into your own execution, unless the king, in that moment, holds out the golden sceptre.

These thirty days. The harem had gone on filling after she was crowned (2:19). She has no reason to think the king still wants to see her, and every reason to remember what happened to the last queen who crossed him.

Knowing the cost. Many readers know what it is to see what ought to be done and exactly what it may cost. Esther’s hesitation is not cowardice. It is honesty about the price, and that is where real courage has to start.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai takes away Esther’s last hiding place: the palace will not save her, and she must now own her people openly.

Do not think to yourself. The decree says all Jews; the palace walls will not stop it, and sooner or later someone will tell Haman who the queen’s cousin is. Silence will only mean that she dies later, having done nothing. That is still the truth about silence: a believer who hides in a comfortable place while the people of God are in danger may keep his comfort for a while, but he has not escaped.

A queen who happened to be a Jew. Mordecai is asking Esther to change which of her names comes first. For five years she has been the queen of Persia who happened, privately, to be a Jew. Now she must become a Jew who happens to be queen, and risk the crown for her people. Timothy Keller often pointed out that this is the choice facing believers who have done well in the world: is faith a private detail of a successful life, or the thing that decides what the success is for? Our culture encourages the first. Faith is fine, provided it stays out of the office, the vote and the dinner party, and many of us have learned to keep our deepest identity quiet wherever it might cost us. Esther shows the price of coming out of hiding, and the reason to pay it: she did not lose herself by owning her people; she found what her life had been for. And she points to the One who did the same at infinite cost. The Son of God owned us publicly and did not hide his name when it cost him everything. He “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people will be delivered whatever Esther does, and yet she may have been placed on the throne for this very hour: both are true.

From another place. First, “relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place”. Mordecai is sure the people will survive, though he does not say how. God had sworn that Israel would last as long as the sun and moon (Jeremiah 31:35–36), and centuries later another Benjaminite would ask, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). The deliverance does not depend on Esther.

You and your father’s house will perish. Her father’s name has been given only once: “Esther the daughter of Abihail” (2:15). As far as we are told, she is all that is left of that house.

For such a time as this. Second, the question. She is an orphan made queen, crowned five years before anyone had heard of Haman’s plan. Mordecai looks at the strange road that brought her to the throne and asks whether this was what it was for.

Who knows? This is the prophets’ phrase for a people under sentence: “Who knows whether he will not turn and relent” (Joel 2:14). The king of Nineveh, in ashes, ordered a fast with the same words: “Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish” (Jonah 3:9). Sackcloth, ashes, fasting, “who knows”, perish: every one is in this chapter. The name of God is not, but the reader of the prophets can hear whom they are hoping in.

A question for every believer. Where has God put you: which family, which job, which room you can walk into that others cannot? It is not an accident, and there may be a moment for which it was all arranged. The One who placed you does not send you in your own strength: his Spirit lives in those who belong to him. And when we fail to speak, as all of us have, Christ has already been faithful in our place, and the way back is confession and his mercy (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. Who or what is “another place”? Later Jewish writers used “the Place” as a name for God, and some hear that here, a veiled way of naming the God the book never names. Others think Mordecai simply means another person or another way of rescue. The words allow both, and Mordecai’s confidence is the same either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — If I Perish, I Perish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther goes to the throne not knowing whether she will live, and asks her people to stand with her as she goes. She tells Mordecai to gather the Jews of Susa to fast on her behalf for three days, night and day, while she and her young women fast as well. Then she will go in to the king, against the law, “and if I perish, I perish” (vv. 15–16). Mordecai goes away and does everything she has ordered (v. 17). The girl who once obeyed him now leads, and the story moves toward the throne room.
verseByVerse.theology: She goes to the throne not knowing whether she will live, and asks her people to stand with her as she goes.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai, "Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther calls her people to fast with her, then resolves to go to the king against the law and leave the outcome with God.

Hold a fast on my behalf. She does not go alone. She asks her people to fast for her, and she and her maids will fast with them: three days without food or water, the Jewish community of Susa and a queen’s household together. It is prayer in everything but the word. And if the fast began as soon as the news came, it fell across Passover, for the decree had been written on the eve of that feast (3:12). The Jews of Susa may have spent that Passover not eating the lamb but fasting.

Though it is against the law. She breaks the king’s law deliberately, because keeping it would mean standing by while her people were killed. Scripture honours that kind of disobedience: Moses’ parents hid their baby, “and they were not afraid of the king’s edict” (Hebrews 11:23). A believer may have to break a human rule to keep a greater duty. What he may not do is pretend the rule does not exist; Esther names it, and accepts the price in advance.

If I perish, I perish. She does not say she will not perish, which would be bravado, or that she hopes she will not, which would be wishful thinking. She will go, and what happens is not in her hands. That is the shape of courage for a believer: not certainty of the outcome, but willingness to act and leave the outcome with God.

Knowing all that would happen to him. It points to a greater scene. In a garden outside Jerusalem another intercessor faced the cost of standing for his people and prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Esther went in not knowing whether she would die. Jesus went “knowing all that would happen to him” (John 18:4), and he did die, under the sentence that was ours. That is why, for those who belong to him, the sceptre is always held out: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Mordecai does everything Esther commands: the girl he raised now leads. A small sentence, and a reversal. In chapter 2 Esther “obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him” (2:20). Now she gives the orders, and he carries them out. From here on it is Esther who takes the lead.

keyVerse.quote: For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
keyVerse.note: Mordecai holds together two truths the whole Bible keeps together: God’s purpose to save his people cannot fail, and the people he has placed are still responsible to act. His closing question becomes the question of the whole book, and of every believer: where has God put me, and for what?

4.reflection:
Mordecai and the Jews met the decree with sackcloth, fasting and a loud cry (vv. 1–3), while Esther’s first response was to send clean clothes (v. 4). When bad news comes, do you tend to cry out to God, or to tidy the trouble away? What does Christ’s promise to those who mourn (Matthew 5:4) offer you?

Mordecai says deliverance will come whatever Esther does, and yet she may have come to the kingdom for this very moment (v. 14). How do God’s sovereignty and our responsibility fit together in this verse, and why does each matter for the way we live?

Esther had to stop being a queen who happened to be a Jew and become a Jew who happened to be queen (v. 13). Where are you tempted to keep your faith a private detail? What might it cost to own it openly, and why is it worth it?

Esther went in uncalled, ready to perish; Christ went knowing he would die, so that we may draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). How should that shape the way you pray, and the risks you are willing to take for others?

5.title: The First Banquet: Grace, Delay, and the Gallows
5.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace.<sup>2</sup>And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.<sup>3</sup>And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom."<sup>4</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."<sup>5</sup>Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared.<sup>6</sup>And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>7</sup>Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is:<sup>8</sup>If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."<sup>9</sup>And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai.<sup>10</sup>Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.<sup>11</sup>And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king.<sup>12</sup>Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king.<sup>13</sup>Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."<sup>14</sup>Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
5.overview:
Where we are. Esther has called the Jews of Susa to fast for three days and resolved to go to the king uncalled, though the law makes it death (4:11, 16). Chapter 5 is the day she goes in. It also shows us Haman at the height of his pride, on the night before everything turns.

The message. God opens the way into the king’s presence and gives his servant both courage and patience, while pride, however high it climbs, is building its own downfall. Esther lives because the sceptre is held out, and then she waits, and her waiting gives the hidden God one more night. Haman has everything and counts it as nothing because one man will not bow, and the tree he raises for Mordecai will be his own.

Why it was said. The scattered Jews of the Persian empire lived under powers they could not control, with no prophet or miracle to reassure them (see the introduction). This chapter showed them God’s hand at work in the timing of things, through a woman’s courage and a proud man’s folly.

How the chapter makes its case. Two scenes face each other. In the first, Esther stands in the inner court, the king holds out the golden sceptre, and offered up to half the kingdom she asks only for a feast; at the feast, asked again, she asks only for another (vv. 1–8). In the second, Haman leaves the feast glad, sees Mordecai at the gate refusing to rise or tremble, and goes home to boast of riches, sons and honours that are all “worth nothing” to him while Mordecai sits there; at his wife’s urging he has a gallows built fifty cubits high (vv. 9–14). Courage and patience stand on one side, pride and rage on the other, and the night between them is the night of chapter 6.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, a link that must not be pressed too hard. Esther entered a throne room where the uncalled could die, and was received only because the king held out his sceptre. Those who belong to Christ come to a greater throne without that fear, because he has gone in before them: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). And by contrast: Haman’s sum, everything minus one man’s bow equals nothing, is the reverse of Paul’s, “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

For us. Courage that waits for the right moment is not cowardice, and God can use our delays as well as our boldness. If anyone’s refusal to honour you spoils everything else you have, the cure is not a gallows of your own making but a fresh look at the honour that is yours in Christ.
5.theology:
Esther approaches the throne uncalled and is received. God works through her courage and through her delay; the extra night she creates is the night he will use. Meanwhile Haman’s pride builds the gallows on which he himself will die.

A Persian king offers half his kingdom; the Father is pleased to give his little flock the whole kingdom (Luke 12:32).
5.examples: The same royal offer of half a kingdom bought John the Baptist's head for Herod's dancer and would buy lives for Esther. And Haman's gallows, built in a single night of spite, would be ready on the very morning after the king could not sleep.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther goes in at the risk of her life, is received by the king’s favour, and then waits. On the third day of the fast she puts on her royal robes and stands where the king can see her; he holds out the golden sceptre, and she touches it and lives (vv. 1–2). Offered anything “even to the half of my kingdom”, she asks only that the king and Haman come to a feast she has already prepared (vv. 3–5). Over the wine he asks again, and again she answers with an invitation, to a second feast tomorrow (vv. 6–8). Her request is delayed by one day, and that one night becomes the hinge of the whole book (6:1).
verseByVerse.theology: She went in under the sentence of death and lived, and then she did not make her request. The one extra night that her delay created is the night on which the whole story turns (6:1).

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace. And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther goes in at the risk of her life, and the king receives her: she touches the sceptre and lives. Anyone who entered the inner court uncalled would die unless the king held out the golden sceptre (4:11), and the king’s heart, as Proverbs says, is “in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1).

On the third day. She has fasted for three days (4:16). Third days in Scripture are often days of deliverance. “On the third day” Abraham saw the mountain where God would provide the lamb (Genesis 22:4); “on the third day he will raise us up,” said Hosea (Hosea 6:2). The Christian reader remembers the third day on which the one under sentence of death came out alive (1 Corinthians 15:4). Esther’s third day is a small one, and we should not make too much of it, but it belongs to the same pattern.

Esther put on her royal robes. Literally, she “put on royalty”. Weak from fasting, she goes as the queen, not as a beggar, and stands where the king’s eyes will fall on her.

Touched the tip of the scepter. The sceptre comes up; she crosses the floor and touches it; she will live. It is the most dangerous walk in the book, and it takes one sentence.

A walk made safe. For those who belong to Christ, that walk has been made safe for good: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16). Esther was received because, that day, the king was pleased with her. We are received because the Father is always pleased with his Son, and we come in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom." And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king knows she would not risk her life for nothing and offers her anything; she asks only for a feast.

Even to the half of my kingdom. The royal way of saying: ask anything. Five centuries later Herod, at his birthday feast, promised a dancing girl “up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23), and she asked for the head of John the Baptist. Esther will use the same offer to ask for lives.

A feast that I have prepared. She brings not a petition but an invitation, and the feast was ready before she went in: she was planning to live. And she asks for Haman to be there. The man who wrote the decree will be at her table when she asks for it to be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared. And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled." Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked a second time, Esther again holds back her request and invites the king and Haman to another feast tomorrow.

As they were drinking wine. The king, the queen and the enemy of the Jews drink together, and only one of the three knows what is at stake. The king asks again (v. 3), and the moment has come.

My wish and my request is. Watch the sentence. It begins like a petition and turns into another invitation. Did her courage fail at the last moment? Did she judge that a second feast, and her promise to speak “tomorrow”, would make the king more ready to grant it? The narrator does not say. What he shows is that the delay gave God one night to work with, and that he used it (6:1).

When the hard thing is not yet said. Many readers know what it is to have meant to say the hard thing and not said it yet. Delay is not always failure, and the God who used Esther’s extra night is patient with ours. The question is whether you go back tomorrow. Esther did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Let a Gallows Fifty Cubits High Be Made
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride can have everything and still have nothing, and it builds its own trap. Haman leaves the queen’s feast “joyful and glad of heart”, but one look at Mordecai, who neither rises nor trembles, fills him with wrath (v. 9). He holds himself in, gathers his wife and friends, and lists his riches, his sons and his honours, crowned by the queen’s invitation, only to declare it all “worth nothing” while that one Jew sits at the gate (vv. 10–13). Zeresh and his friends advise a gallows fifty cubits high and an early word with the king, and the idea pleases him (v. 14). He goes to bed with the gallows rising, on the night the king will lose his sleep.
verseByVerse.theology: The tree Haman raised that night for a righteous Jew will stand in the next chapter with a different body on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai. Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man who will not stand for him turns Haman’s joy to fury, and he takes his grudge home.

Joyful and glad of heart. One sentence takes him from delight to rage. One man at the gate spoils a private dinner with the king and queen. “Neither rose nor trembled”: Mordecai, under sentence of death, is not afraid of him.

Haman restrained himself. He controls his face in public and goes home to talk about it. That is how grudges grow: not in outbursts, but nursed in private and retold to friends who take our side.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king. Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king. Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman has riches, sons, rank and the queen’s favour, and counts it all as nothing while one Jew will not bow.

The splendor of his riches. He tells his wife and friends what they already know: wealth, ten sons (9:7–10), rank above every official, and, crowning it all, the queen’s invitation. He thinks it is the height of his career. It is the trap.

How pride does its sums. Yet all of it is “worth nothing to me”. Everything, minus one man’s bow, equals nothing. That is how pride does its sums, and why it can never be satisfied: there will always be one person who does not bow.

Two ways of counting. Set Haman’s sentence beside Paul’s: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Both men count everything as nothing because of one person: Haman, because of a man he hated; Paul, because of the One he loved. The first sum leads to a gallows. The second leads to Christ.

Status anxiety at the king’s gate. Haman is not a monster from another world. He has what the philosopher Alain de Botton called status anxiety, one of the quiet sicknesses, de Botton argued, of modern life. A society that says anyone can rise by merit implies that those who have not risen deserve their place, so we watch our rank nervously, as if it measured our worth. Underneath, he suggested, the hunger for status is a hunger for love, which is why one unbowed head can ruin a whole day. Run the test on yourself: is there one person whose coolness, success or refusal to give you your due spoils everything else you have? If your worth hangs on other people’s regard, everyone who withholds it has a hand on your throat,. The cure is not to try harder at contentment, nor to stop caring about honour, but to receive an honour no one at the gate can take away. The King of heaven has spoken his delight over his Son, and “he has blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). Someone who knows that can walk past a man who will not bow, and let him sit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman’s household advises a towering gallows for Mordecai, and the idea pleases him: pride is building its own downfall.

A gallows fifty cubits high. Fifty cubits is about 75 feet (some 23 metres), far higher than any execution needed: Haman’s rage made visible, so that all Susa could see what happened to a Jew who would not bow. Mordecai would die before breakfast, and Haman would enjoy the queen’s dinner.

This idea pleased Haman. The book’s favourite phrase (1:21; 2:4) pleases the one man it should have frightened. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The gallows was ready by morning (6:4), and that night the king could not sleep (6:1).

Another tree, outside Jerusalem. Many Christian readers cannot see a tree raised to kill a righteous Jew without thinking of another: “Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree” (Acts 5:30). Haman’s tree would end by holding the guilty man; that one held the Innocent in the place of the guilty.

Uncertain wording. “Gallows” is literally “tree” or “wood”, and “hanged” can describe a body fixed on a stake. Persians often executed by impaling, so this may have been a tall stake rather than a scaffold with a rope; we cannot be sure. Either way it was an instrument of public death, meant to be seen.

keyVerse.quote: And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
keyVerse.note: The chapter, and the book, hang on this moment. Esther has gone in uncalled under the shadow of death (4:11, 16), and she lives only because the king holds out his sceptre. It is a small picture of the welcome every sinner needs, and which those who are in Christ have been given for good (Hebrews 4:16).

5.reflection:
Esther prepared a feast before she went in (v. 4), as someone who expected to live, yet she had said “if I perish, I perish” (4:16). How do faith, courage and careful planning belong together when you face something frightening?

Esther held back her request for a day (vv. 7–8), and God used the delay (6:1). When have you put off saying something hard? How can you tell wise timing from fear?

Haman calls everything he has “worth nothing” while one man will not bow (v. 13). Is there someone whose coolness or success spoils your contentment? What difference does it make that God “has blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6)?

Esther risked her life to approach the king; Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to the throne of grace “with confidence”. What keeps you from coming freely to God in prayer, and what has Christ done about it?

6.title: The Night the King Could Not Sleep
6.text: <sup>1</sup>On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.<sup>2</sup>And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."<sup>4</sup>And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him.<sup>5</sup>And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."<sup>6</sup>So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"<sup>7</sup>And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor,<sup>8</sup>let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set.<sup>9</sup>And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"<sup>10</sup>Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned."<sup>11</sup>So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."<sup>12</sup>Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.<sup>13</sup>And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."<sup>14</sup>While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
6.overview:
Where we are. Esther has invited the king and Haman to a second feast, and Haman has gone to bed with a gallows rising for Mordecai (5:14). Chapter 6 is the night between, the turning point of the whole book: from here the danger that has grown since chapter 3 begins to run backwards.

The message. God governs the world through the ordinary and the overlooked, and in his own time he humbles the proud and lifts up the humble. A king’s sleepless night, a page read aloud, a faithful deed forgotten for years, a man arriving at exactly the wrong moment: none of it is chance. Haman comes to ask for Mordecai’s death and ends by leading Mordecai through the city in the king’s robes, and even his own household can see that he will fall.

Why it was said. The first readers were a scattered minority with no miracles to point to (see the introduction). They needed to know whether faithfulness that goes unnoticed is wasted, and whether God still steers events he does not visibly enter. This chapter answers both.

How the chapter makes its case. The king cannot sleep, has the chronicles read, and learns that Mordecai, who saved his life, was never rewarded (vv. 1–3). At that moment Haman enters the court to ask for Mordecai’s hanging; asked how to honour “the man whom the king delights to honor”, he assumes it is himself and designs a royal parade (vv. 4–9). He is ordered to do it all for Mordecai the Jew, and leads him through the square proclaiming the honour with his own mouth (vv. 10–11). Mordecai goes back to the gate; Haman goes home in mourning, hears from his wife and advisers that he will surely fall, and is hurried away to Esther’s feast (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. Here the link to Christ is the character of God that this night reveals. The God who lifted Mordecai and brought Haman down is the God who exalts the humble, a pattern that reaches its height in his Son, who humbled himself to the cross and whom “God has highly exalted” (Philippians 2:9). The Father delights to honour him, and through him those who serve him: “If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him” (John 12:26). And the hidden hand of this night belongs to the one in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17).

For us. Nothing done for God is forgotten by him, even when people forget it for years. If you lie awake, lie awake knowing that he does not sleep; and leave your honour in his hands, for those who grab it, like Haman, end up leading someone else’s horse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — On That Night the King Could Not Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In one sleepless night God brings a forgotten act of faithfulness back into the light. The king cannot sleep and orders the royal chronicles read to him, and the reader reaches the record of how Mordecai uncovered the eunuchs’ plot against the king’s life (vv. 1–2). Asked what honour Mordecai received for it, the servants reply, “Nothing has been done for him” (v. 3). Nothing here is miraculous, and nothing is accidental: the night is the one after the gallows was ordered, the page is the one that mattered, and the deed is remembered at the moment it can do the most good.
verseByVerse.theology: The gallows had been ordered and the queen's second feast was hours away. The book never says who kept the king awake.

verseByVerse.quote: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the very night the gallows goes up, the king cannot sleep, and the cure he chooses brings Mordecai’s forgotten deed to light.

The king could not sleep. That night: after Esther’s first feast, while Haman’s gallows was being made. Literally, the king’s sleep fled. Daniel records the same of another king, on another night when a Jew’s life hung in the balance: Darius “spent the night fasting … and sleep fled from him” (Daniel 6:18).

The book of memorable deeds. The king’s cure for insomnia was to have the court records read aloud. In Hebrew it is the book of remembrances, and the deed filed and forgotten in 2:23 is in it. Malachi spoke of another such book: “a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD” (Malachi 3:16).

Who took the king’s sleep? The Hebrew does not say. When the book was translated into Greek, the translators could not bear the silence and wrote that the Lord took sleep from the king. The Hebrew leaves it unsaid and trusts the reader: we are not told, and we know. “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). The emperor of the world lay awake that night because the Keeper of Israel was awake.

In everyday life. Many readers have lain awake with something that will not leave them. The king’s sleepless night was not wasted, and neither are ours: the One who does not sleep uses the hours when we cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai saved the king’s life and received nothing; now, on the one morning it matters most, the king finds out.

It was found written. Out of years of records from 127 provinces, the reader happened to reach this page. Nobody went looking for it.

Years unrewarded. The plot was uncovered some time after Esther became queen in the seventh year (2:16, 21); we are now in the twelfth (3:7). For as long as five years the man who saved the king’s life had received nothing, though Persian kings prided themselves on rewarding those who served them. And the reward was delayed until the one morning when it would do the most good: the morning Haman came to ask for his death.

Unthanked, not forgotten. Faithfulness that went unthanked is not lost. “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10). The reward may be years in coming, and it will come at the right time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — The Man Whom the King Delights to Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The proud man plans his own honour and is made to give it to the man he meant to kill. Haman arrives at dawn to ask for Mordecai’s hanging and is called in before he can speak (vv. 4–5). Asked what should be done for “the man whom the king delights to honor”, he is sure it means himself, and designs a parade in the king’s own robes, on the king’s own horse, led by a noble crying out the man’s honour (vv. 6–9). The king orders him to do it all for Mordecai the Jew, leaving nothing out, and Haman himself leads the horse through the city square (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The gallows was ready, and Haman spent the morning leading Mordecai's horse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him. And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the very moment the king wants to honour Mordecai, the one man in the court is Haman, come to ask for his death.

Who is in the court? The king has spent the night hearing about Mordecai; Haman has spent it planning his death. Both converge on the throne room at dawn, Haman early because the gallows is finished and he wants permission before Esther’s feast. He never gets to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked how to honour the man the king delights in, Haman assumes it can only be himself.

Whom would the king delight to honor more than me? The narrator lets us hear Haman’s thought, and it is the whole man in one sentence. In the world of the proud there is only one person who deserves honour.

Exalted and humbled. Jesus told of a guest who took the place of honour at a wedding feast and was moved down in front of everyone: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Haman is about to live out the first half of that sentence in the streets of Susa, and Mordecai the second.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor, let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set. And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman designs the honour he craves: not money, but to be seen in public as if he were the king.

Let royal robes be brought. He does not ask for money or land, which he has. He wants the king’s own clothes, the king’s own horse, and a public proclamation.

One of the king’s most noble officials. He has designed every detail, including the noble who will lead the horse. Without knowing it, he has just described the task he himself will be given on the worst morning of his life.

Like Joseph in Egypt. A reader of Genesis knows this scene. When Pharaoh raised Joseph, the Hebrew prisoner, he “clothed him in garments of fine linen”, set him in his chariot, “And they called out before him, ‘Bow the knee!’” (Genesis 41:42–43). Another exile in a foreign court is lifted up by a king’s robe and a public cry.

Uncertain wording. “On whose head a royal crown is set” most naturally refers to the horse, and ancient carvings from the region show royal horses wearing a crest or tall ornament on the head, which is probably what is meant. Some take the crown to be for the rider, but the grammar favours the horse.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned." So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman must give his dream honour, in every detail, to Mordecai the Jew, and proclaim it with his own mouth.

Do so to Mordecai the Jew. Every phrase lands: Mordecai; “the Jew”; “who sits at the king’s gate”, the very place where he refused to bow; “Leave out nothing.” And the king says “Mordecai the Jew” without a flicker. The decree to kill the Jews is still posted in every province, and he has not connected the two. He honours a Jew in the morning under a law that will kill him in Adar.

He dressed Mordecai. Haman dresses him with his own hands, walks at the horse’s head and shouts the proclamation he had written for himself, and the whole city sees it.

A King who delights to honour. There is a greater King who delights to honour. At the Jordan his voice said of his Son, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and after the cross “God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). That delight reaches those who belong to his Son: “If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him” (John 12:26). The servant of Christ whom the world overlooked will be clothed in a righteousness not his own and welcomed into God’s city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — You Will Surely Fall Before Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reversal has begun, and even Haman’s own household can see where it ends. Mordecai goes quietly back to his post at the king’s gate, while Haman hurries home mourning, with his head covered (v. 12). The same wife and friends who advised the gallows now tell him that if Mordecai is a Jew, he will not overcome him but will surely fall before him (v. 13). Before he can recover, the king’s eunuchs arrive to hurry him to Esther’s feast (v. 14). The chapter that began with a sleepless king ends with a stumbling enemy on his way to the table where he will be unmasked.
verseByVerse.theology: Even Haman's wife can see which way the story is going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai goes quietly back to work; Haman goes home in grief and shame.

Mordecai returned to the king’s gate. The honour has not gone to his head, and it has not changed his situation: the decree still stands. He returns to his post, as the faithful do.

With his head covered. Covering the head was a sign of grief and shame (see mourning customs); David went up the Mount of Olives “weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered” (2 Samuel 15:30). In chapter 4 it was Mordecai who mourned in the streets. Now it is Haman.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same household that advised the gallows now tells Haman that against a Jew he cannot win.

You will not overcome him. In a book that never names God, one of the clearest statements that the Jews cannot be destroyed comes from the enemy’s own wife and advisers. They seem to have known something of this people’s story (see the introduction on the old war with Amalek). God had said to Abraham, “I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse” (Genesis 12:3), and even pagan advisers could see that those who set themselves against this nation fell.

Before whom you have begun to fall. The word comes twice: “begun to fall … surely fall”. In the next chapter it comes a third time, when Haman is found “falling on the couch” where Esther lay (7:8).

verseByVerse.quote: While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman is hurried off to Esther’s feast with no time to recover, and the timing of the whole chapter shows whose hand is on events.

Hurried to bring Haman. “Hurry,” said the king (v. 10); Haman “hurried” home (v. 12); now the eunuchs hurry him to the feast. Invited as the queen’s honoured guest, he goes to her table with his wife’s words still in his ears.

God’s hand in the timing. That is how the book shows God’s hand: not by naming him, but by the timing. Any one of the night’s coincidences could be luck; all of them together, on the one night that mattered, make the reader say what the book never says.

What providence means. The word for what this chapter shows is providence: God’s care for everything he has made, keeping it in being and steering it to his ends, usually through ordinary things like a sleepless night and a page in a ledger. It is neither chance, Haman’s creed (cast the lot and see), nor fate, a blind machine that grinds on whatever anyone does. It is a Person, wise and good, holding every thread and working through human choices, not around them. The One who holds the threads has a name this book never writes, and the New Testament writes it plainly: in Christ “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). The hands that keep the world were pierced for us, which is why a believer can say with Joseph, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). See also Providence in the Theological Dictionary.

In everyday life. Most of us live as practical believers in chance: we trust what we can plan and control, and panic when we cannot. Tonight, look back over one day, name one ordinary thing in it (a delay, a meeting, a word that came at the right moment), and thank God that it was not luck.

6.theology:
God is unnamed and unmistakable: a king's sleep taken, a page found, a man in the court at the wrong moment, all on the one night that mattered. Faithfulness left unrewarded for years is remembered at the right time.

The proud man is humbled and the humble man exalted, and the King who delights to honour his Son honours those who serve his Son.
6.examples: The ironies pile up. Haman came to ask for a hanging and was asked to plan an honour, and the king honoured Mordecai the Jew while his decree to kill the Jews still stood.

keyVerse.quote: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.
keyVerse.note: The whole book turns on this sentence. Before it, Haman’s power grows; after it, everything is reversed. God is not named, yet the reader knows who kept the king awake, for “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).

6.reflection:
A sleepless king, a page read aloud, Haman’s early arrival: none of these is a miracle, yet together they change everything (vv. 1–5). Where can you look back and see God’s hand in the timing of ordinary events in your own life?

Mordecai’s service went unrewarded for years (vv. 2–3). How do you respond when faithfulness goes unnoticed, and how does Hebrews 6:10 help?

Haman assumed the honour must be for him (v. 6). How does pride shape the way we hear what others say, and the way we read situations?

After his moment of glory, Mordecai simply went back to the gate (v. 12). What does that teach about receiving honour? How does the humbling and exaltation of Jesus (Philippians 2:5–11) change the way we seek it?

7.title: The Second Banquet: Esther Speaks, Haman Falls
7.text: <sup>1</sup>So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther.<sup>2</sup>And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>3</sup>Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request.<sup>4</sup>For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."<sup>5</sup>Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"<sup>6</sup>And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.<sup>7</sup>And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king.<sup>8</sup>And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.<sup>9</sup>Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."<sup>10</sup>So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
7.overview:
Where we are. The night of reversal is over. Mordecai has been paraded in the king’s robes, and Haman, told by his own household that he will fall, has been hurried to Esther’s second feast (6:12–14). Chapter 7 is the climax of the story, the hour Esther has been moving towards since she said, “if I perish, I perish” (4:16).

The message. Evil is exposed and falls into the pit it dug, while the one who stands with God’s condemned people at her own risk is heard. Esther finally speaks, naming herself with her people and naming their enemy to his face; the king’s anger turns on Haman, and he is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. Yet the chapter ends with the decree still in force, for removing the enemy does not undo the sentence.

Why it was said. For Jews who had lived under Haman’s decree, and for every later generation that kept Purim (see the introduction), this chapter answered the question whether those who plot against God’s people have the last word. They do not: “His mischief returns upon his own head” (Psalm 7:16).

How the chapter makes its case. At the second feast the king asks a third time, and Esther pleads for her life and her people’s, quoting the very words of the decree: “to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated” (vv. 1–4). The king demands to know who has dared to do it, and she points across the table: “A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!” (vv. 5–6). The king storms into the garden; Haman, begging the queen for his life, is found fallen on her couch, and his face is covered (vv. 7–8). A eunuch mentions the gallows standing at Haman’s house, Haman is hanged on it, and the king’s wrath abates (vv. 9–10).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, a pattern turned inside out. Haman’s tree, raised for a righteous man, held the guilty one; the cross held the Righteous One in the place of the guilty, for “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). As Haman’s weapon turned on him, so at the cross the enemy’s weapon became his defeat: Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). And where Esther placed herself under her people’s sentence, Christ went all the way and “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

For us. Evil that seems unstoppable is never beyond God’s reach, so we need neither despair nor take revenge into our own hands. And before we join the king in pointing across the table, we should look for our own seal on the decree, and run to the One who bore our condemnation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther speaks at last, standing openly with her condemned people and naming their enemy to his face. At the second feast the king asks a third time for her request (vv. 1–2). She asks for her own life and her people’s, and uses the decree’s own words, “to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated”, adding with great tact that she would have kept silent over mere slavery (vv. 3–4). The king demands to know who has dared to do this, and she points across the table: “A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!” The man who raged because a Jew would not tremble before him now trembles before a Jewish queen (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The queen who had hidden her people for five years says I and my people in one breath, and names the man at the table. The king asks who dared to do what he himself had signed.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther. And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the second feast the king asks Esther a third time for her request, and the moment she has waited for has come.

The king again said to Esther. This is the third time he has asked (5:3, 6). Haman is at the table, the same Haman who this morning led Mordecai’s horse through the city and was told by his wife that he would fall. Only the queen knows what she is about to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther pleads for her life and her people’s, giving up her secret and placing herself under their sentence.

Let my life be granted me. The king asked for her wish and her request, and she answers in exactly those terms: my life, and my people. She puts herself first so that the king will feel it; the threat is to his own queen. Then, “my people”: the secret she has kept since the day she entered the harem (2:10) is given up in two words.

To be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. These are the three verbs of Haman’s decree, word for word (3:13): she quotes the king’s own law back to him. And “sold” means someone paid for this (3:9).

If we had been sold merely as slaves. Even at the edge of death she is tactful: she would not have troubled the king over mere slavery. But this is killing, and she speaks with the courtesy of a queen and the courage of someone who has already said, “if I perish, I perish” (4:16).

Uncertain wording. The last clause is among the hardest in the book: “affliction” can also mean “enemy”, and the word for “loss” occurs in Hebrew only here. It may mean, as the ESV takes it, that slavery would not have been worth troubling the king about, or (as older versions take it) that the enemy could never make good the king’s loss. Either way Esther pleads in terms of the king’s own interest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?" And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king demands to know who has dared to do this, and Esther names the man sitting at the table.

Who is he, and where is he? Part of the true answer is: you. The king handed Haman the signet ring and said, “the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you” (3:11). He never asked which people. It is a picture of how easily the powerful sign things and forget them, and how outraged they become when what they signed touches someone they love.

This wicked Haman! After five years of silence and two days of feasts, she says his name with him sitting there. The man who was filled with wrath because a Jew would not tremble before him (5:9) trembles before a Jewish woman.

Why is outrage so satisfying? The king’s fury is real, but as long as the evil has a name and a face across the table, he never has to look at the seal on the decree. We too can be eloquent about the cruelty of others, another generation, party or nation, and the heat of the denunciation quietly reassures us that we stand on the right side of the line. Outrage can be moral seriousness; it can also be a way of not looking in the mirror. Scripture keeps turning the king’s question round. When David burned with anger at the rich man in Nathan’s story, the prophet answered him in four words: “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

The One who would not say “Not me”. The gospel goes further than exposure. There was One who could have pointed at every one of us and said, with perfect truth, “Not me.” Instead he “was numbered with the transgressors” and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Those who know that can afford to find their own name on the decree, and they no longer need a Haman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enemy falls into the pit he dug, though his decree survives him. The king storms out into the palace garden, and Haman stays to beg the queen for his life; when the king returns, Haman has fallen on her couch, and the king takes it as an assault (vv. 7–8). His face is covered, and Harbona the eunuch reminds the king of the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, “whose word saved the king” (v. 9). Haman is hanged on it, and the king’s wrath abates (v. 10). Justice is done to Haman, but the law he wrote is still in force, and the next chapter must deal with it.
verseByVerse.theology: The tree Haman raised for a righteous man held the guilty one. At the cross it was the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king. And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king storms out; Haman begs the queen for his life, and his fall onto her couch seals his fate.

The king arose in his wrath. Perhaps he also needs time to think, since the decree has his seal on it. Haman sees his death in the king’s face and does the one thing left: he begs. The man who required every knee at the gate to bend is on his knees before a Jew.

Falling on the couch. Guests reclined on couches to eat. Haman, pleading, throws himself down at the queen’s couch just as the king walks back in. “Falling”: the word Zeresh used only hours before, “you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him” (6:13). To the king it looks like an assault on the queen.

They covered Haman’s face. That morning Haman had covered his own head in shame (6:12). Now others cover it, and it means death.

Uncertain wording. No other source describes this custom at the Persian court, though the Romans veiled condemned traitors, and some think the words mean that Haman’s face fell. The plain reading is likeliest: from that moment he is a dead man.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant mentions the gallows, proof that Haman had plotted against the man who saved the king.

Harbona, one of the eunuchs. Harbona was one of the seven eunuchs sent to fetch Vashti (1:10). He adds the detail that settles it: the gallows was built “for Mordecai, whose word saved the king”. Last night’s reading is known to the whole court. Haman had planned to hang the man the king was honouring, and the gallows stood at his house for all Susa to see.

verseByVerse.quote: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman dies on the tree he raised for Mordecai, and the king’s anger is satisfied, but the decree lives on.

The gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. The Psalms had long since described it: “He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head” (Psalm 7:15–16). The tree Haman raised for the righteous man held Haman.

The reversal ran the opposite way. At the cross the tree that should have held the guilty held the righteous One: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”, for “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). And as with Haman’s gallows, the enemy’s weapon turned on the enemy: “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). On that tree Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). “The wrath of the king abated”, as it had when his anger at Vashti cooled (2:1), satisfied by the death of the guilty man. God’s wrath against his people was satisfied by the death of One who was not guilty: “we have now been justified by his blood”, and “much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9).

The decree still stands. Yet the chapter ends with a problem unsolved. Haman is dead; his decree is not. It is still posted in every province, sealed with the king’s ring, and cannot be repealed. The next chapter is about what can be done with a law that cannot be undone.

7.theology:
The enemy dies on the gallows he built for another, and Esther gives up her safety to stand with her people.

Haman's tree held the guilty; Christ's cross held the Righteous in the place of the guilty, and there the enemy's weapon became his defeat and God's wrath toward his people was turned away (see on vv. 9-10).
7.examples: The man who demanded that every knee bend to him ended the day begging a Jewish woman for his life. Yet the chapter closes on unfinished business: Haman died, and his decree did not.

keyVerse.quote: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
keyVerse.note: In one sentence the story’s great reversal is complete: the gallows meant for the righteous man holds his enemy, and the king’s anger is stilled. It points by contrast to the cross, where the Righteous One hung in the place of the guilty and God’s wrath against his people was turned away (Romans 5:9).

7.reflection:
Esther gave up the secret she had kept for years and said, “I and my people” (vv. 3–4). Where might God be calling you to identify openly with Christ and his people, even at a cost?

The king was outraged at a plot he himself had signed (vv. 5–6; 3:10–11). Why is it easier to denounce wrong in others than to see our own part in it, and how does the gospel free us to look honestly?

Haman fell into the pit he had dug (v. 10; Psalm 7:15–16). How does this encourage believers facing injustice, and why does it still give us no licence to take revenge ourselves (Romans 12:19)?

Haman’s tree held the guilty; Christ’s cross held the innocent in the place of the guilty (Galatians 3:13). What does that exchange mean for you, and how might you thank God for it this week?

8.title: The Edict of Reversal: Light and Joy
8.text: <sup>1</sup>On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.<sup>2</sup>And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.<sup>3</sup>Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews.<sup>4</sup>When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king.<sup>5</sup>And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king.<sup>6</sup>For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people?
