And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
8.overview:
Where we are. Haman is dead, hanged on his own gallows, but his decree still stands, sealed with the king’s ring and set for the thirteenth of Adar (7:10; 3:13). Chapter 8 deals with a problem the king himself cannot solve: a law that cannot be revoked.

The message. When a sentence of death cannot simply be cancelled, God provides a counter-word with the same royal authority, and mourning is turned into joy. Esther, safe herself, pleads in tears for her people; the king lets her and Mordecai write a second decree in his name, giving the Jews the right to defend themselves; and as the news runs along the roads of the empire, the Jews have “light and gladness and joy and honor”.

Why it was said. The first readers, and every generation that kept Purim (see the introduction), lived as a minority under laws they did not write. The chapter showed them that the God of their fathers can work through the machinery of an empire, turning its own decrees and couriers to the rescue of his people.

How the chapter makes its case. Haman’s house goes to Esther and his ring to Mordecai, now known as her kinsman (vv. 1–2). Esther falls at the king’s feet and begs him to revoke Haman’s letters; he cannot, but he allows her and Mordecai to write as they please in his name (vv. 3–8). On the twenty-third of Sivan the new edict goes to every province in every language, the Jews’ own included, permitting them to gather and defend their lives on the very day set for their destruction (vv. 9–14). Mordecai goes out in royal robes, Susa shouts for joy, the Jews feast, and many from the peoples declare themselves Jews (vv. 15–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes, by pattern and by promise. The need: a sentence that cannot be revoked must be answered by another word from the king. Our sentence was just, as Haman’s was not, and God did not ignore it; he “condemned sin in the flesh” of his own Son (Romans 8:3) and then spoke the answering word: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The pattern: Esther, safe herself, went back in for her people; Christ “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). The promise: Gentiles attaching themselves to the Jews (v. 17) are a first glimpse of the multitude “from every nation” before the Lamb (Revelation 7:9).

For us. Do not rest content in your own safety while others remain under sentence; use whatever access you have to plead for them. And when guilt or fear tells you the old decree still stands, read the second decree again, written in the King’s own name and sealed with his Son’s blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — An Edict Sealed with the King's Ring Cannot Be Revoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haman is dead, but his law is alive, and only a new word from the king can answer it. On the same day the king gives Haman’s house to Esther, and Mordecai, revealed as her kinsman, receives the signet ring that sealed the decree (vv. 1–2). Esther, safe herself, falls at the king’s feet in tears and pleads for Haman’s letters to be revoked, for she cannot bear to see her kindred destroyed (vv. 3–6). The king replies that a decree sealed with his ring cannot be revoked, but gives Esther and Mordecai authority to write another in his name and seal it with the same ring (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Haman was dead and his law was alive.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her. And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the same day, the enemy’s house and the enemy’s authority pass to the Jews he meant to destroy.

The house of Haman. The man who planned to plunder every Jewish house in the empire has lost his own to a Jew. “The sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous” (Proverbs 13:22). And the cousin at the gate is brought into the king’s presence as family.

His signet ring. The ring that sealed the death of the Jews (3:10) is on a Jew’s hand. Joseph received a ring the same way: “Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand” (Genesis 41:42). The man who would not bow to Haman now holds Haman’s authority and Haman’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews. When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king. And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king. For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though she is safe, Esther goes back to the king in tears, because she cannot live with her people’s danger.

Esther spoke again to the king. She could have stopped: her enemy was dead, her life safe. But the decree still hung over every Jewish family in the empire, and she goes back in, not in royal robes to a feast, but at his feet in tears.

The golden scepter. The sceptre is held out again, and she is careful where she lays the blame: on “the letters devised by Haman”, not on the king who sealed them.

How can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred? This is the heart of an intercessor: she is safe, and she cannot live with their danger. Paul felt the same for the same people: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart … for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9:2–3).

He did not stay safe. Christians have long seen in her a faint likeness of a greater Intercessor. The Son of God did not stay safe in his Father’s presence: he came down, laid down his life for his people, and now “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). She pleaded with a king who might refuse. He pleads with a Father who always hears him (John 11:42).

Is our own safety enough for us? The love that grieves for those not yet safe is not ours by nature; it is the love of the One who first grieved over us, poured into our hearts by his Spirit (Romans 5:5). In practice it may mean using whatever access we have, as she used hers, for people who have none: praying by name for persecuted believers, or speaking to those in power on their behalf. “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews. But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king cannot cancel his own sealed decree, but he can authorise a second one, with the same name and ring, to stand against it.

Cannot be revoked. The king himself states the problem. The law of the Medes and Persians, which deposed Vashti (1:19), now binds the king to a massacre he no longer wants (compare Daniel 6:15). What he can do is let them write another decree, with his name and ring on it.

A likeness to the gospel. The likeness must be stated carefully. Haman’s decree was wicked; the law’s sentence on us is just. But the principle holds: a sentence that cannot be revoked must be answered, not ignored. God did not cancel the sentence on sin or pretend it was not there. “By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3), and then he issued the word that answers it: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
verseByVerse.note: Compare Daniel 6:8, 12, where the same rule binds Darius.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Light and Gladness and Joy and Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The counter-decree races across the empire, and mourning gives way to light and joy. On the twenty-third of Sivan Mordecai’s edict is written to all 127 provinces, in every script and language, and to the Jews in their own (vv. 9–10). It allows the Jews to gather and defend their lives against any armed force that attacks them on the thirteenth of Adar, the day Haman’s lot had chosen, and the swiftest royal couriers carry it out (vv. 11–14). Mordecai leaves the palace in royal robes and a great golden crown, and Susa, once thrown into confusion, shouts for joy (v. 15). Everywhere the edict reaches there is feasting, and many from the peoples declare themselves Jews (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same roads that carried mourning now carry feasts.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language. And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring. Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai’s edict goes out through the same imperial machinery as Haman’s, and this time to the Jews as well.

On the twenty-third day. Two months and ten days after the first decree (3:12), with nearly nine months still to run before the thirteenth of Adar.

Also to the Jews. The same scribes, provinces and imperial post, with one addition: this decree goes to the Jews as well, in their own script and language, so that every Jewish family can read with their own eyes that they may live. The Persian royal post was famous (the Greek historian Herodotus said nothing mortal travelled faster), and the news of life goes on the best horses in the empire.

Uncertain wording. The words behind “bred from the royal stud” are rare Persian loanwords whose exact sense is unknown; clearly these were the king’s finest horses.

verseByVerse.quote: saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods, on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new decree gives the Jews the king’s permission to defend themselves, in the very words Haman had used against them.

To destroy, to kill, and to annihilate. Put this beside 3:13: Mordecai has turned Haman’s decree round, verb for verb. The first decree licensed anyone to kill Jews. This one licenses Jews to defend themselves against anyone who tries.

Was this a licence for revenge? No. It is aimed at “any armed force of any people or province that might attack them”, and limited to one day. When the day comes, chapter 9 speaks of men killed in Susa (9:6, 15) and of “those who hated them” in the provinces (9:16), and three times says the Jews laid no hand on the plunder they had been permitted (9:10, 15, 16). The likeliest reading is that the right granted was self-defence, and that they used it with restraint (see the introduction on whether such events are patterns for the church).

Uncertain wording. “Children and women included” is hard to place. The ESV suggests that the attackers’ families might be struck too, mirroring 3:13; but the words may belong with “them”, meaning the Jews’ own children and women whom an armed force might attack. Either way the decree is defensive.

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies. So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The counter-decree is posted everywhere and carried at top speed, so that every Jew can be ready on the appointed day.

Publicly displayed to all peoples. Beside the old notice in every town square goes up a new one, sent in the same hurry as before (3:15). Anyone who read the first and sharpened a knife would now read the second.

To take vengeance on their enemies. Here this means lawful retribution on a decreed day against those who attacked, not private revenge. The Hebrew word is used of a ruler’s justice as well as of personal revenge, and the decree gives no licence beyond the day and beyond those who came to kill.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who sat at the gate in sackcloth comes out of the palace in royal robes, and the city rejoices.

Royal robes of blue and white. Blue and white, fine linen and purple: the colours of the palace hangings (1:6). The man who sat at the gate in sackcloth and ashes (4:1) walks out dressed like the palace itself. The last time he wore royal robes it was for a morning, with Haman leading his horse (6:11). These are his own.

The city of Susa shouted and rejoiced. When Haman’s decree went out, “the city of Susa was thrown into confusion” (3:15). Now it “shouted and rejoiced”. “When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices” (Proverbs 11:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor. And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word of grief is answered by a word of joy, and people from the nations begin to join themselves to the Jews.

Light and gladness and joy and honor. Count the words. When the first decree arrived, the Jews had four: “mourning … fasting and weeping and lamenting” (4:3). Now they have four others. “Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (Psalm 97:11). Anyone who has lived under a sentence (a diagnosis, a debt, a guilt that would not go away) and heard it answered knows how they felt.

Wherever the king’s command and his edict reached. This is the phrase of 4:3: the couriers who had carried mourning along those roads now carried feasts.

For fear of the Jews. The book is honest about the motive, and some no doubt only wanted to be on the winning side. But the prophets had seen a day when the nations would join this people: “ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, ‘Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you’” (Zechariah 8:23). The Christian reader sees where that ends: “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9).

Uncertain wording. “Declared themselves Jews” translates a single verb found only here. It may mean that they became Jews, joining the people and its faith, or that they claimed to be Jews or took the Jews’ side. The motive given, fear, suggests that for many it was the latter, though some may have truly turned to Israel’s God.

8.theology:
A decree that cannot be revoked must be answered by a decree of equal authority. God has done with the just sentence on sinners what the Persian king could not do with an unjust one: carried it out on his own Son and declared that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ (see on vv. 7-8).

Esther will not rest in her own safety while her kindred are in danger. Mourning is turned to light and joy, and the nations begin to attach themselves to God's people, as the prophets foresaw.
8.examples: The reversals come one after another: Haman's house belonged to a Jew that same day, and the ring that had sealed the death of the Jews was on Mordecai's hand. Esther, safe herself, went back in, in tears, for her people.

keyVerse.quote: But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king’s ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king’s ring cannot be revoked.
keyVerse.note: Here are the chapter’s problem and its answer in one sentence: the first decree cannot be revoked, but the king’s name and ring can stand behind a second. God neither ignores nor cancels his just sentence on sin; he answers it in Christ with a better word: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

8.reflection:
Esther was safe, yet she went back to the king in tears for her people (vv. 3–6). Whose danger, physical or spiritual, ought to trouble you more than it does, and what access do you have that you could use on their behalf?

The king could not revoke his decree, but he could issue another (vv. 7–8). How does this help you understand what God has done with our sentence in Christ (Romans 8:1–3)? Where do you still live as if the first decree stood?

The Jews’ grief was answered word for word with joy (vv. 16–17; compare 4:3). How can a church celebrate God’s deliverance in a way that honours him and draws others in?

Many joined the Jews out of fear (v. 17). What draws people to God’s people today, and what ought to?

9.title: The Great Reversal: Victory and the Feast of Purim
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.<sup>2</sup>The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples.<sup>3</sup>All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.<sup>4</sup>For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.<sup>5</sup>The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.<sup>6</sup>In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men,<sup>7</sup>and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha<sup>8</sup>and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha<sup>9</sup>and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha,<sup>10</sup>the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.<sup>11</sup>That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king.<sup>12</sup>And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."<sup>13</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."<sup>14</sup>So the king commanded this to be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.<sup>15</sup>The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder.<sup>16</sup>Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder.<sup>17</sup>This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness.<sup>18</sup>But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth day, making that a day of feasting and gladness.<sup>19</sup>Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another.<sup>20</sup>And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far,<sup>21</sup>obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year,<sup>22</sup>as the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.<sup>23</sup>So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.<sup>24</sup>For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them.<sup>25</sup>But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.<sup>26</sup>Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. Therefore, because of all that was written in this letter, and of what they had faced in this matter, and of what had happened to them,<sup>27</sup>the Jews firmly obligated themselves and their offspring and all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days according to what was written and at the time appointed every year,<sup>28</sup>that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, in every clan, province, and city, and that these days of Purim should never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor should the commemoration of these days cease among their descendants.<sup>29</sup>Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew gave full written authority, confirming this second letter about Purim.<sup>30</sup>Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth,<sup>31</sup>that these days of Purim should be observed at their appointed seasons, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther obligated them, and as they had obligated themselves and their offspring, with regard to their fasts and their lamenting.<sup>32</sup>The command of Esther confirmed these practices of Purim, and it was recorded in writing.
9.overview:
Where we are. Haman is dead and Mordecai holds his ring, but Haman’s decree still stands, and chapter 8 has answered it with a second decree letting the Jews defend themselves. Now the thirteenth of Adar arrives, the day Haman’s lot chose eleven months before (3:7, 13), and with it the climax of the book.

The message. On the very day appointed for the destruction of God’s people, “the reverse occurred” (v. 1). God, still unnamed, turns the enemy’s day of triumph into his people’s day of rescue, and then has the rescue written down to be remembered for ever with feasting and generosity. The enemy’s own lot gives the feast its name: what was meant for their death becomes the story they tell their children.

Why it was said. The chapter explains why the scattered Jews keep Purim, a feast not found in the law of Moses (see the introduction). Every generation that kept it lived as a minority among the nations, often hated, and needed to know that the God who never appears in the story had kept them alive.

How the chapter makes its case. The day comes, and the Jews gather in every province, helped by officials who fear Mordecai (vv. 1–4). They strike those who come to kill them, in Susa five hundred men and Haman’s ten sons, but touch no plunder (vv. 5–10). At Esther’s request a second day is given in Susa and the sons’ bodies are hanged; in the provinces the Jews defend their lives, and three times the narrator insists that they took no spoil (vv. 11–16). Then they rest and feast, the provinces on the fourteenth and Susa on the fifteenth (vv. 17–19). Mordecai fixes the two days as a yearly feast of gifts to one another and to the poor (vv. 20–22), the story is retold in brief and the feast named Purim after Haman’s lot (vv. 23–28), and Esther confirms it in writing (vv. 29–32).

Where it leads. Chiefly by pattern, and honestly so, for the book makes no promise of a Messiah. The shape of this day is the shape of the cross, where the enemies of God thought they had won and the reverse occurred (1 Corinthians 2:8; Colossians 2:15). It leads by promise kept as well: God preserved the people through whom “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). And it exposes a need. This deliverance still needed a sword, and Amalek’s old hatred ended only in blood. Christ ends hostility another way, “killing the hostility” by his own death (Ephesians 2:16), and gives his church a feast of remembrance of its own (Luke 22:19).

For us. When the day you dread arrives, God is not absent because he is unseen. Remember what he has done, and keep the memory with joy, at the Lord’s Table and in generosity, so that no one is left out of the feast. And never take up the sword of Esther 9 for Christ’s kingdom: our enemies are not flesh and blood, and our victory has already been won for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the day appointed for their death, God’s people find the tables turned. The thirteenth of Adar comes, the day Haman’s lot chose, and “the reverse occurred” (v. 1). The Jews gather in every city to meet those who sought their harm, and no one can stand against them, for fear of them and of Mordecai has fallen on peoples and officials alike, the very officials who once posted Haman’s decree (vv. 2–4). They strike their enemies, five hundred in the citadel of Susa and Haman’s ten sons, but leave the plunder untouched (vv. 5–10). This is a fight for life, not for gain, and Saul’s old failure against Amalek is not repeated.
verseByVerse.theology: The day chosen by lot for the Jews' destruction became the day of their deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day chosen for the Jews’ destruction, God, unnamed, turned everything round.

The reverse occurred. On the day Haman’s dice chose eleven months before (3:7, 13), “the reverse occurred”: literally, “it was overturned”. The book sums up its whole message about God in one phrase. The narrator does not say who reversed it, and he does not need to: every reader who has come this far knows whose hand turned it.

On that day too. The cross was the day the enemies of God thought they had won. “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). On that day too, the reverse occurred.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples. All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials who posted Haman’s decree now protect its victims, for fear of the Jews and of Mordecai has fallen on everyone.

The fear of them had fallen. They gathered, as the second decree allowed (8:11). This is what Rahab said to the spies at Jericho: “the fear of you has fallen upon us” (Joshua 2:9). Something about this people, when God was with them, made their enemies lose heart.

All the officials of the provinces. The same officials who had posted Haman’s decree now protected its intended victims. The man who a year before had sat at the gate in sackcloth (4:1) was the most feared man in the empire’s administration.

Grew more and more powerful. This echoes David’s rise: “And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him” (2 Samuel 5:10). The narrator stops before the last clause; the reader who knows it will finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When their enemies came to kill them, the Jews defended themselves, and for once the power was not with those who hated them.

The Jews struck all their enemies. This is the hard verse of the book, not to be hurried past. Look first at who is struck: “their enemies”, “those who hated them”, “those who sought their harm” (v. 2). Haman’s decree was still law. In every province men had waited eleven months to kill Jewish families and take their houses, and on that day they came. The Jews met them. “Did as they pleased”, the book’s recurring phrase (1:8), here means the power had changed hands.

Was this right? A plain reader will ask, and should. Three things can be said honestly. First, this was not Haman’s massacre simply turned round. Haman’s law, never cancelled, let anyone kill every Jew, children included (3:13), and on that day men came to use it. The Jews were allowed to meet “any armed force of any people or province that might attack them” (8:11), and the dead are named as “those who hated them”. To defend one’s family from men coming to kill them is not murder (Exodus 22:2 assumes a householder may defend his house). Second, the narrator reports without cheering: there is no victory song over the slain. Third, Scripture records Esther and Mordecai truly without asking us to approve every request, and the second day in Susa (v. 13) remains hard.

What the book wants us to see. God did not let his people be wiped out, for the promise of a Saviour ran through them (Genesis 12:3). None of it is a pattern for the church, which is given no sword to wield for Christ (Romans 12:19). Christ won his victory not by killing his enemies but by dying for them.

Where Christians differ. Many hold that the Jews acted justly, in lawful self-defence. Others think the narrator quietly records an excess, especially the second day (v. 13), and shows God saving his people in spite of their faults. Others read it as the last act of the LORD’s war with Amalek (Exodus 17:16).

This commentary’s view. Self-defence against those who came to kill them, with striking restraint over the plunder. The Amalek background explains the book’s interest in Haman’s house but licenses nothing today: these are records, not patterns (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.quote: In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men, and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha, the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haman’s sons fall with his house, and the Jews refuse the plunder Saul once took from Amalek.

The ten sons of Haman. In the Hebrew scrolls these ten names are written in a column by themselves, one under another. Haman had boasted to his friends of “the number of his sons” (5:11). Here they are, counted.

They laid no hand on the plunder. The second decree had allowed them plunder (8:11), and they did not touch it; the book says so three times (vv. 10, 15, 16). Why the insistence? Saul, sent against Amalek, “spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen” (1 Samuel 15:9), and Samuel asked him, “Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?” (1 Samuel 15:19). Saul lost his kingdom over the plunder of Amalek. Now a Benjaminite of the line of Kish (2:5) faces the Agagite’s house again, and this time no one takes a thing. This was not greed dressed up as self-defence: they fought for their lives and went home with nothing else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — They Laid No Hands on the Plunder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fighting ends in rest, and the rest in a feast. The king hears the toll in Susa and asks Esther, for the fourth time, what more she wants (vv. 11–12). She asks for a second day in the capital and for the bodies of Haman’s sons to be hanged in public, a request the narrator records without comment (vv. 13–14). In Susa and across the provinces the Jews defend their lives against those who hated them, and again they refuse the plunder (vv. 15–16). Then they rest, on the fourteenth in the provinces and on the fifteenth in Susa, and the days of rest become days of feasting, gladness and gifts (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The sons of Kish, facing the house of Agag, refused exactly what Saul had taken.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king. And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king tells Esther the toll in Susa and, for the fourth time, invites her request.

Now what is your wish? This is the fourth time the king asks her (5:3; 5:6; 7:2). The king who once gave away a people without asking their name (3:8–11) now reckons up the dead of his own capital and asks the Jewish queen what more she wants.

verseByVerse.quote: And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows." So the king commanded this to be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther asks for another day in Susa and the public hanging of Haman’s dead sons, and the king grants it.

Let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also. Many readers are troubled by this, and honestly so. We are not told why Esther asked. What the text shows is that there were still enemies in Susa: the next day the Jews killed three hundred more (v. 15).

Let the ten sons of Haman be hanged. The sons were already dead (v. 10); hanging their bodies was the ancient way of making a public end of a house, so that no one could doubt that Haman’s line was finished. The narrator neither praises the request nor condemns it. Esther is not presented as sinless anywhere in this book, and we are not asked to make her so. Like the whole chapter, it is no pattern for the church (see the note on v. 5).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder. Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Across the empire the Jews defend their lives and again take nothing for themselves.

Killed 75,000 of those who hated them. Seventy-five thousand is a terrible number, and the text does not make it pleasant, though across 127 provinces it describes many local attacks beaten off, not one battle. But see how it is framed: “to defend their lives”, against “those who hated them”, and with no hand laid on the plunder. Like Abram (Genesis 14:23), they would not be made rich by it.

Got relief from their enemies. They “got relief”, and then “rested” (v. 17). Moses had put three things together: rest from enemies, the end of Amalek, and a command never to forget (Deuteronomy 25:19). All three are in this chapter.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament gives 15,000; the Hebrew, which our Bibles follow, has 75,000.

verseByVerse.quote: This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness. But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth day, making that a day of feasting and gladness. Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The feast celebrates not the fighting but the rest that followed, and it is shared.

Rested on the fifteenth day. The Jews of Susa, who fought two days, rested on the fifteenth; those of the unwalled “rural towns”, on the fourteenth. Hence Purim’s two dates, and the later custom of keeping the second day in walled cities.

A day of feasting and gladness. The feast is not the day of the fighting but the day after, the day they rested. Purim does not celebrate killing. It celebrates rest: the morning a people woke up and found they were still alive.

Gifts of food to one another. A generation later Nehemiah’s hearers were told the same: “send portions to anyone who has nothing ready” (Nehemiah 8:10, 12). Joy is meant to be shared.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — These Days Should Be Remembered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A rescue that is not remembered is soon lost, so this one is written down and made a feast for ever. Mordecai writes to all the Jews, near and far, binding them to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year, the month turned from sorrow into gladness, with gifts to one another and to the poor (vv. 20–22). The story is retold in a sentence, Haman’s plot falling back on his own head, and the feast is named Purim after his lot (vv. 23–26). The Jews bind themselves, their children and all who join them to keep it in every generation (vv. 27–28), and Queen Esther confirms it in writing with her own authority (vv. 29–32).
verseByVerse.theology: Amalek's memory ended, and the memory of deliverance was written down to last.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year, as the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai makes the days of rescue a yearly feast of gladness and of gifts to one another and to the poor.

Turned for them from sorrow into gladness. Letters go down the same roads again, this time about a feast. “Turned” says again what verse 1 said: “the reverse occurred”. The psalm says it of one man: “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (Psalm 30:11). Mordecai had worn the sackcloth (4:1) and then the royal robes (8:15).

Your sorrow will turn into joy. Jesus promised it to his disciples the night before the cross: “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20).

Gifts to the poor. The deliverance was to be remembered with generosity. Nobody was to be left out of the feast because they could not afford it. Those who have been given so much give.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them. For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them. But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole story is retold in brief: Haman’s plot fell back on his own head.

Should return on his own head. They had already begun to feast; Mordecai made it law. Then the whole book in a sentence: Haman’s “evil plan … should return on his own head”. And again the psalm: “His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends” (Psalm 7:16).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “when it came” can equally be read “when she came”, and the King James Version takes it so (“when Esther came”); the feminine pronoun may mean Esther or the plot. Either way, the turning point was the queen who went in uncalled, “if I perish, I perish” (4:16), and the plot that died when it was brought into the king’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. Therefore, because of all that was written in this letter, and of what they had faced in this matter, and of what had happened to them, the Jews firmly obligated themselves and their offspring and all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days according to what was written and at the time appointed every year, that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, in every clan, province, and city, and that these days of Purim should never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor should the commemoration of these days cease among their descendants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The feast is named after Haman’s lots, and the Jews bind themselves and their children to keep it for ever.

They called these days Purim. Purim means “lots”: Haman’s lots (v. 24). The very device he used to choose the day of their death gave its name to the feast of their deliverance. His dice are remembered every year, and only as the joke that God made of them: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). This is probably why the book was written at all: to tell later generations of scattered Jews why they keep these two days, and that they had been kept alive by a God the book never names.

All who joined them. The people who had declared themselves Jews (8:17) are included in the feast.

The memory of Amalek. God had once told Moses to “write this as a memorial in a book” that he would blot out the memory of Amalek (Exodus 17:14). Here Haman’s house, the last we hear of Amalek’s line, is gone, and Israel’s deliverance is written down to be remembered.

The church’s feast of remembrance. The church has a feast of remembrance too, instituted on the night before the greatest reversal of all: “do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Should Christians keep Purim? It was a Jewish festival not commanded in the law of Moses. Christians are free to remember it, but no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Its message belongs to us: God keeps his people, unseen, through ordinary events.
verseByVerse.note: Purim is still celebrated by Jews each year, with the reading of Esther.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew gave full written authority, confirming this second letter about Purim. Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth, that these days of Purim should be observed at their appointed seasons, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther obligated them, and as they had obligated themselves and their offspring, with regard to their fasts and their lamenting. The command of Esther confirmed these practices of Purim, and it was recorded in writing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Queen Esther adds her own royal authority, and the feast is fixed in writing.

The daughter of Abihail. Her father’s name for the second time in the book (2:15). Esther, the orphan girl who hid her people, now writes to all of them, in her own name, with the authority of a queen.

In words of peace and truth. Peace and truth, with fasts and lamenting turned into feasts: all of it is in Zechariah’s promise that “the fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth … shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace” (Zechariah 8:19). And the fasts are not forgotten. The feast remembers the sackcloth that came before it.

Recorded in writing. It is written in a book, like Mordecai’s deed (2:23) that was read on the sleepless night (6:1). God’s name was never written in it. His faithfulness is on every page.

Uncertain wording. “This second letter” may follow Mordecai’s (v. 20) or confirm it. “With regard to their fasts and their lamenting” is unclear: Purim may be fixed like fasts the Jews had already taken on themselves, or may remember the mourning of chapter 4. Either way the feast stands, in memory of grief turned to joy.

9.theology:
The day chosen for destruction is overturned into the day of deliverance, and the enemy's own lot names the feast. The Jews defend their lives and refuse the plunder Saul once took; the feast is kept on the day of rest, not of battle.

Sorrow turned into joy is what the gospel brings, and the church keeps its own feast of remembrance. But the church does not take up the sword for Christ: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4). In Esther the old enmity between Agag and Israel ends with the sword. In Christ God ends hostility another way, reconciling enemies to himself and to one another through the cross, thereby killing the hostility (Ephesians 2:16), so that the feast of the gospel is kept by Jew and Gentile together.
9.examples: Purim is kept on the day they rested, not the day they fought, with gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor, so that no one is left out of the joy.

keyVerse.quote: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king’s command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.
keyVerse.note: This is the whole book in one phrase: “the reverse occurred”. The day chosen by lot for the Jews’ destruction becomes the day of their deliverance, and the narrator does not need to say who overturned it. The same hidden hand turned the day of the cross, when the enemies of God thought they had won, into the day of our salvation.

9.reflection:
“The reverse occurred” (v. 1), yet God is not named. Looking back, where have you seen a situation turned round in a way you can only put down to God? What helped you see his hand afterwards rather than at the time?

Three times the narrator says the Jews “laid no hand on the plunder” (vv. 10, 15, 16). Why does he insist on it? What does it look like to stand against wrong without using it to enrich yourself or settle scores?

Purim was kept on the day of rest, not the day of fighting, with gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor (vv. 17–22). How could our remembering of what God has done in Christ, at the Lord’s Table and in our homes, become as joyful and as generous as this?

This chapter troubles many readers. How would you explain to a friend why the church today is given no sword for Christ’s kingdom (2 Corinthians 10:4), and what weapons it has instead?

10.title: Mordecai's Greatness and the Hidden Hand Revealed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.<sup>2</sup>And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?<sup>3</sup>For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
10.overview:
Where we are. The feast of Purim has been fixed in writing (9:29–32), and the story is over. Three verses remain, an epilogue in the manner of the books of Kings, closing the account of Ahasuerus’s reign and of the Jew who stood beside him.

The message. The book that opened with a king showing off “the riches of his royal glory” (1:4) ends with a servant using his power for others: Mordecai “sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people” (v. 3). The rescue was real, but the empire goes on and the Jews are still its subjects. Their safety rests not on Persia but on the unseen God who put his servant where he was needed.

Why it was said. The first readers lived on under foreign kings, taxed and far from Jerusalem (see the introduction). The ending told them that their deliverance was history recorded in the royal chronicles, and that faithful service inside a pagan empire was both possible and good.

How the chapter makes its case. The king taxes land and coastlands, and the empire’s ordinary business goes on (v. 1). His deeds, and Mordecai’s honour, are written in the chronicles of Media and Persia, the same records in which Mordecai’s forgotten deed was once filed (v. 2; 2:23; 6:1). And Mordecai, second only to the king, is great among the Jews and loved by them, because he used his place for their welfare and peace (v. 3).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Like Joseph in Egypt and Daniel in Babylon, Mordecai is the faithful servant raised beside the throne for the good of his people. But he is only second, his greatness ends with his life, and the book closes with God’s people still paying tribute to a foreign king. Esther leaves us waiting for a greater One: not second to the King but seated “at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3), who “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17), and of whose kingdom “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

For us. Whatever influence God has given you, at work, at home or in public life, is given for others: seek their welfare and speak peace. And when the world goes on as if nothing has changed, remember that God has written down the story of his people, and his King reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — He Sought the Welfare of His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book closes quietly, with power put to its proper use. The king taxes his empire to its coasts, a reminder that the Jews are still subjects of a Persian throne (v. 1). His deeds and Mordecai’s high honour are written in the royal chronicles, where Mordecai’s forgotten service was first recorded, so the reader knows this is history (v. 2). Last of all, the Jew second to the king is great among his people and loved by them, because he sought their welfare and spoke peace to them (v. 3). The book that opened with a king displaying his own glory ends with a servant spending his for others.
verseByVerse.theology: The book that opened on a king displaying his glory closes on a Jew using his power for the good of others. God is not named in the last sentence either. Peace is.

verseByVerse.quote: King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The empire goes on: the deliverance was real, but it was not yet the kingdom of God.

Imposed tax on the land. It is an odd way to end, and true to life. The empire goes on; the taxes are collected; the Jews are still subjects of a Persian king. God’s people still live in someone else’s empire, as in every age until the King comes.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “tax” (mas) usually means forced labour elsewhere; here it is probably tribute. Why the writer mentions it is not said, perhaps simply to show the empire carrying on.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai’s honour is written in the royal records, and the deed once forgotten is now told in full.

Are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles? That is how the books of Kings close each reign: “are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?” (1 Kings 14:29). Esther ends like a king’s story, and the name beside the emperor’s is a Jew’s. It is the same book in which Mordecai’s unrewarded deed was filed (2:23) and read aloud on the sleepless night (6:1). The man who got a line in the annals now has a full account. The chronicles are lost, though Persian tablets name officials called Marduka.

A better book. God keeps “a book of remembrance” of those who fear him (Malachi 3:16). No service done for him is lost, even if no king ever reads it.

verseByVerse.quote: For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai ends second only to the king, and the last words are about what he did with his power: he sought his people’s good.

Second in rank to King Ahasuerus. Mordecai is second in the empire, as Joseph had been in Egypt: “only as regards the throne will I be greater than you” (Genesis 41:40). Haman used power to destroy a people; Mordecai used it to seek their good.

He sought the welfare of his people. This is the language of Jeremiah’s letter to the first exiles: “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). The book, true to itself to the last line, gives us Jeremiah’s words but leaves out the prayer and the name of the LORD. The reader who has come this far can supply both.

He shall speak peace to the nations. A greater King has one at his right hand who is not second to him but one with him (Hebrews 1:3), and of whom Zechariah said, “he shall speak peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10). “He came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). Mordecai spoke peace to his own people. Christ speaks it to everyone who comes to him, and his reign has no end.

Uncertain wording. “The multitude of his brothers” may also mean “most of his brothers”: some Jewish interpreters took it that not everyone approved of him, but most translations read it as the goodwill of the many.

The Greek additions. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles continue the book after this verse with Mordecai’s dream. These are additions made in the Greek translation; the Hebrew book ends here, as Protestant Bibles do.

10.theology: True greatness is power used for the good of others. Mordecai spoke peace to his people; the King whom Zechariah promised speaks peace to the nations.
10.examples: The last chapter opens with taxes, and the last word of the book is peace.

keyVerse.quote: For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
keyVerse.note: The book’s last words are about what power is for. Haman used his place to destroy a people; Mordecai used his to seek their welfare and speak peace. It is a small picture of the King greater than Mordecai, of whom Zechariah said, “he shall speak peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10).

10.reflection:
The book ends with taxes and an empire still in charge (v. 1). Why might the writer close so ordinarily? How do you live with deliverances that are real but are not yet the end of the story?

Mordecai’s deed was once forgotten, and now his honour is written down in full (v. 2; compare 2:23; 6:1). How does it help you to know that God remembers what others overlook (Malachi 3:16; Hebrews 6:10)?

Mordecai used his position to seek “the welfare of his people” and to speak peace (v. 3). What influence has God given you, and whose welfare could you seek with it this week?

Mordecai was second to the king. How does he help you see the greatness of Christ, who is not second to God but one with him, and who speaks peace to all who come to him?
